items.question: How do I calm down and wait on God so I can hear from Him?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this directly. Calming down is itself the way the greatest miracle was stirred up — Jesus had the agitated crowd sit down, and the word to you is to be careful for nothing, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God (Philippians 4:6) [1]. A flustered person running from one emergency to another will not think clearly or hear from God, so give yourself time to calm down in His presence — sometimes it takes several days, as the Levites stayed at the tabernacle door seven days for their consecration [1].

Waiting on God is a skill few have, and if you do not wait on Him you will not hear from Him; they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength (Isaiah 40:31) [4]. Be still and know that I am God (Psalm 46:10) — silence helps you hear from Him, and it was when there was silence that a voice came [2]. Set yourself targets, even hours of prayer, following Jesus who continued all night in prayer to God (Luke 6:12) [5], and time yourself, remembering Jesus asking Peter, "What, could ye not watch with me one hour?" (Matthew 26:40) [7]. You can also wait with fellow ministers, as the prophets and teachers at Antioch ministered to the Lord and fasted and the Holy Ghost spoke (Acts 13:1-2) [7], and with the congregation, gathering the people and sanctifying a fast (Joel 2:15-16) [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Stir It Up*, chapter 12 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*, chapter 9 of *The Privilege* and chapter 24 of *Church Growth*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 46:10; Isaiah 40:31; Daniel 1:4; Joel 2:15-17; Matthew 26:40; Luke 6:12; Acts 13:1-2; Philippians 4:6.

items.question: Why is it dangerous to pretend to be strong when I'm actually struggling?
items.text:
It's dangerous because pretending keeps you from the help you need. If your pastor knows you are weak, he can pray for you, but if you pretend to be mighty, how can he know you need help? [1][2] When you appear strong even though you are weak, nobody can help you, and you are preventing your own deliverance by covering what needs help [1][2].

The picture given is Samson: mighty in ministry, killing thousands, yet weak in his private life — mighty publicly but the opposite in private [1][2]. And as a pastor, there are people he doesn't particularly need to visit because they are strong, but when there is a weak one, he rushes there because he needs attention; when you look strong like Samson, you won't get any attention [1][2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Duality* and chapter 11 of *Spiritual Dangers*.

items.question: What mistakes do pastors usually make that hurt their ministry?
items.book: The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make
items.text:
Friend, our books name several mistakes that wound a ministry. Choosing to bear little fruit is one of them — pastors leave fruitful places for places where there is no one to preach to, when God is glorified by much fruit, as John 15:8 says [1]. Wrong priorities also kill a ministry: it matters more to build your own church than to have a nice car, and giving priority to the rich while setting aside the young, the children and the poor causes a church to die quickly [4].

Turning into a Pharisee is another — caring about where you sit and being called by titles, as Matthew 23:6-7 describes [2]. Downplaying humility is a grave mistake, since except we become as little children we shall not enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 18:3) [8]. And being slow about ministry is dangerous, for our times are not all the same, as Jesus said, "My time is not yet come: but your time is alway ready" (John 7:6) [7].

There are also the marks of a disappointing shepherd: choosing the sacrifices you make instead of obeying, no longer considering yourself a sheep who needs leading, and not remaining small in your own eyes, as Samuel told Saul in 1 Samuel 15:16-17 [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 3, 7, 8 and 9 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make* and chapter 31 of *The Art of Shepherding*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:16-17; Matthew 18:3; Matthew 23:6-7; John 7:6; John 15:8.

items.question: Why do people hear the same sermon differently?
items.text:
People hear the same sermon differently because everyone hears at a different level. Some only hear your accent, others the grammar, others the stories or jokes, and still others hear the principles and Scriptures — while some hear the Spirit speaking and receive wisdom and guidance from the Holy Spirit [1]. Jesus knew this, which is why He said, "Hearing they cannot hear" [1].

Hearing rightly also requires faith. The gospel was preached to some, but "the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it" (Hebrews 4:1-2) [8]. Judas sat at the table when Jesus spoke of His betrayer, yet the message did not benefit him because he did not hear with faith [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 12 of *Steps to the Anointing* and chapter 16 of *Seeing And Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 4:7; Matthew 13:14-15; Luke 22:22-23; Hebrews 4:1-2.

items.question: How can I recognize when someone is using flattery or food to lead me into sin?
items.text:
Our books speak clearly about flattery, but they do not address food being used to lead someone into sin, so I'll stay with what they say about flattery.

Flattery is excessive praise given insincerely to gain favor for oneself, and it works ruin [3]. Watch for people who excessively praise you and your ministry, because flattery is a sign of disloyalty and of someone who will eventually leave you; their praises are a mask for their true intentions [1]. Scripture warns us plainly: "there is no faithfulness in their mouth... they flatter with their tongue" (Psalms 5:9) [1], and "a flattering mouth worketh ruin" (Proverbs 26:28) [3]. Jude 16 describes such people as grumblers who speak arrogantly, "flattering people for the sake of gaining an advantage" [1].

The danger is what it does inside you: flattery makes you think you are what you are not, it is an injection of pride, and pride goes before a fall [2]. It can even make ordinary men think they are God, though no man is a god and all men are mortal [2]. So be on guard when someone tells you there is no one like you, or hails you with grand titles [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 3 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 5:9; Proverbs 26:28; Zechariah 1:5; 1 Thessalonians 2:5; Jude 16.

items.question: Why is my church not growing?
items.book: Why Is This Church Not Working?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this weight, pastor. Our books name several possible reasons, and I'd gently lay them before you.

It may be that you have a low capacity for studying — people who do not study books on ministry and church growth will not have growth, and a failing church is a revelation of a lack of knowledge, wisdom and understanding [2]. It may be that you are not diligent, passive and laid-back, needing constant supervision, for pastors who make a constant effort to accomplish something are the only ones who have working churches [3]. It may be the location of your church, for you are not to worship just anywhere but in the place which the Lord shall choose (Deuteronomy 12:13-14), and perhaps it is time to relocate [4]. It may be that you are using the wrong church growth strategy, since a house is built by wisdom and by a series of steps (Proverbs 24:3-4) [5]. Or it may be that your vision is not a burning vision, for in the absence of a burning vision for a large church you will never have real church growth [7].

Alongside these, the books also say that church growth is warfare — something is fighting you, that is why your church is not growing, and pastors who are not prepared to go to war cannot have church growth [1]. And they say to attempt great things for God and attempt to grow a church, for the church of God can grow if you nurture it, and you are destined to multiply (Jeremiah 30:19) [6]. They also encourage patience: don't be in a hurry, for no tree grows from a seed into a large tree overnight [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *The Double Mega Missionary Church*, chapters 11, 12, 17 and 18 of *Why Is This Church Not Working?*, chapter 11 of *Attempt Great Things for God*, chapter 1 of *Church Growth* and chapter 7 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 12:13-14; Proverbs 22:29; Proverbs 24:3-4; Proverbs 29:18; Jeremiah 30:19; Matthew 13:31-32; Mark 6:2; Acts 16:5; 2 Timothy 2:15.

items.question: What diseases can you get from having sex before marriage?
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this. Fornication is sexual intercourse before marriage [3][5], and the germs that cause sexually transmitted diseases gain access into you when you commit fornication [1][2]. Among the diseases named are Gonorrhoea, Syphilis, Non-Specific Urethritis, liver diseases from Hepatitis B, Herpes Genitalis, Vaginitis, Lymphogranuloma venereum, Soft Sore (Chancroid), urinary tract infection, and cancer of the cervix, since frequent sex at an early age predisposes you to it [1][2].

Fornication can also bring death: it will kill you if you acquire HIV, and unless God works a miracle, you may die of AIDS [1][2]. The books add that if you wait till you marry before having sex, you may save yourself from all these diseases [1][2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Spiritual Dangers* and chapters 2 and 3 of *All About Fornication*.

Scriptures referenced: Jeremiah 3:15; Ephesians 5:3.

items.question: How can I know if I'm on the wrong path in life?
items.text:
Our books speak to this in a few ways. One test is the company on the road: the broad way has many people on it and the narrow way has few, and it is the road with a lot of people on it that the world sees as the right road — yet Jesus warned that you must be among the few who choose Him [2]. Another test is your conscience, that quiet inner voice that checks you when you go wrong; your heart has the ability to condemn you for wrongdoing (1 John 3:20-21), and anyone who claims to be led by the Spirit but does not listen to his conscience is doomed to tragedy [4].

There is also the matter of the end of the road: there is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death (Proverbs 14:12), and the way of heaping up riches and the way of pleasure are not the way to Heaven or to God [7]. And if you have committed your way to God (Proverbs 3:5-6), He directs your paths — blocking certain doors and making it impossible for you to go on certain roads, so that you flow in a particular direction [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 50 and 65 of *How You Can Preach Salvation* and chapters 19 and 24 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 3:5; Proverbs 14:12; Ecclesiastes 4:8; Matthew 7:13-14; John 14:4-6; Acts 24:16; 1 John 3:20-21.

items.question: What should I do when one of them is a leader I trained?
items.text:
When a leader you trained leaves, our books speak to both sides of it. On your part, guard your heart against bitterness, for "many people are bitter and angry at those who leave them" [1], and bitterness is a root that troubles and defiles many (Hebrews 12:15) [1]. Remember too that God is not stranded: "sometimes the departure of a person heralds the arrival of God's choice for you," and God raised up David only after Saul's heart departed from following the Lord [5]. So open your heart to the new relationships God will bring [5].

On the departing leader's part, the books are clear about how such a person should leave: if he must resign, he should resign alone and not influence other ministers to leave with him [2]; he should not win the hearts of people beforehand by making special friends among vital church members, leaving behind a confused group who must choose between their relationship with him and their commitment to the church [2]; he should be grateful to the church he is departing and not spread bad stories about it afterward, for "whoso rewardeth evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house" (Proverbs 17:13) [2]; and he should not "muddy" the waters he drank from, lest he foul the residue with his feet (Ezekiel 34:18) [2]. If he intends to set up a church, he must declare his intentions to the senior minister, discourage others from following him, and not set up within a 10-mile radius of where he used to be [2].

The books also warn what such a breakaway often becomes: a pastor who had time to influence the people can deceive and lead away much of the congregation [3], and renegade ministers often do as Jeroboam did, appointing "the lowest of the people" to high positions, which makes nonsense of spiritual authority and confuses the flock (1 Kings 12:28-31) [3]. One such departure can release a "domino spirit of rebellion" into a team of pastors, as others follow the example and start splinter churches, leaving hundreds of confused members not knowing which little group to belong to [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*, chapter 4 of *Those Who Forget*, chapter 8 of *The Mega Church* and chapters 3 and 10 of *Those who leave you*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 16:3; Numbers 16:8-9; 1 Kings 12:28-31; Proverbs 17:13; Ezekiel 34:18.

items.question: What does it mean to build a church on a deep foundation?
items.text:
Building on a deep foundation means going deeper so you can build something great for God — tall, majestic structures are only possible by going deeper [1]. Jesus told of the man who dug deep and laid his foundation on a rock, so that when the flood beat against the house it could not shake it, because it was founded on a rock (Luke 6:47-49) [1]. The deeper and stronger the foundation, the greater and taller the building [2].

Those foundations include salvation through the blood and cross of Jesus Christ, faithfulness and loyalty, evangelism and outreach, teaching and sticking to the word of God, tithes and offerings as the financing for God's work, and the truth that God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life [1][2]. These must never be belittled or set aside, and they must be protected, for "if the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?" (Psalm 11:3) [2][3][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Going Deeper and Doing More*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 11:3; Luke 6:47-49.

items.question: What does it mean when someone constantly accuses others and tries to control them?
items.text:
What you're describing sounds like what the book calls witchcraft — the use of any power other than the power of God to control people [1]. One way control gets established is by accusing and pestering someone with words; through persistent accusations, controlling people stop you from doing things they don't like, and over time they achieve a level of control over your life [1]. A person with a controlling spirit is described as a witch, wielding that power through relentless accusations [2].

The book also says such accusers may not even realize what they've moved into — sometimes those accusing you do not know they have entered the realm of witchcraft [1]. And accusations are often manifestations of other things in the accuser's heart: fear, since the great fears people carry are manifested through accusations [2], or hatred, since your accuser is the one who hates you most [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 4 of *Those Who Accuse You*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 25:24-25; John 15:25.

items.question: What are creeping things in the spiritual sense and how do I pray against them in my church?
items.text:
Creeping things are things that sneak up on you without you realising it — spiritually, things that move upon us stealthily, so that great changes take place over a long period of time and most people hardly notice [2]. The book names four that creep upon all churches: deception, wrong attitudes like laziness, complacency and unbelief, familiarity, and the shifting of priorities, such as becoming health and educational organisations instead of missionary societies [2]. Deception is a creeping thing — the church in Europe did not degenerate overnight; the spirit of deception crept on it slowly [1][2].

As for praying against them, intercessory prayer is what deals with the law of creeping things [2]. Intercessory prayer is necessary to keep out these spiritual creepers, and it will fight that creeping familiarity that kills the flow of the Spirit [1]. So keep interceding for your church, pastor — that is the weapon given for these things.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 21 of *Transform Your Pastoral Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 1:25-26.

items.question: How do I start a new church in a town where we have no members?
items.text:
Begin by counting the cost, because it will not be easy and not many people want to identify with a small thing [5]. You do not need a crowd to start: two or three gathered in His name is enough, as Matthew 18:20 says [6]. One pastor willing to obey God is all that is needed, and the basics are simply praying, witnessing and following up converts [6].

Do not be financially desperate in these early stages; find a job and start as a lay person rather than depending on the new church for your survival [1][2]. Do not rent an expensive hall, and do not keep the church's money in your house or personal account [3][4]. Do not be discouraged by fluctuating attendance, for that is how sheep behave [3][4]. And do not allow anyone to demean your efforts, for though your beginning is small, your latter end will be greatly increased [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *The Mega Church*, chapter 20 of *Church Planting* and chapter 3 of *Those Who Pretend, Intimidate And Are Familiar*.

items.question: What does the Bible say about being a shepherd like Jesus?
items.text:
Being a shepherd is a privilege, not just a job — Jesus Himself was a shepherd and called Himself the Good Shepherd, so you are joining Him in His chosen profession [1]. The work involves visiting people, praying for them, counselling with the word of God, and preaching and teaching [1]. A shepherd is a caring, loving guide whom God has called to look after sheep [5], and the word "shepherd" is interchangeable with "pastor" — so when Jesus said "I am the good shepherd," He was really saying "I am the good pastor" [6][7].

A good shepherd leads his sheep, being practically available so they can see and learn from him, doing first whatever he wants them to do [2][7]. He is apt to teach and feeds the flock, and he has an interest in evangelism — leaving the ninety-nine to seek the one gone astray, as Matthew 18:12 says [8]. Jesus said, "I came to seek and save that which is lost" (Luke 19:10), so a good shepherd seeks to save sinners [8]. And a shepherd is privileged to help people prosper, for "The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1) [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *The Privilege*, chapters 1, 7, 9 and 13 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd* and chapter 8 of *Church Growth*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 23:1-6; Psalms 95:6-7; Ecclesiastes 9:10; Matthew 9:36; Matthew 18:12; Luke 19:10; John 10:3; John 10:11; John 10:14; Ephesians 4:11 and 2 more.

items.question: How does the grace of God help my ministry reach more people and get support?
items.book: How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry
items.text:
The grace of God is what makes your gift available to many people — it's why some ministries have great patronage, many readers, and many supporters [1]. It's also the grace of God that causes much support to abound toward your ministry; when great grace was upon the early church, no one among them lacked, and they sold their possessions and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet (Acts 4:33-35) [1].

The grace of God also determines how far your ministry will go — it's why some pastors have larger churches and others smaller, why some evangelists have larger crowds [2]. And it can be seen by the great numbers who respond: when the hand of the Lord was with them at Antioch, a great number believed and turned to the Lord, and Barnabas saw the grace of God there for himself (Acts 11:19-24) [3]. So pray for the grace of God to work powerfully in your life and ministry [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 17 of *How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: Acts 4:33-35; 2 Timothy 1:8-9; 2 Timothy 2:1; Titus 2:11-12.

items.question: What is true forgiveness?
items.text:
True forgiveness is releasing all hurts, bitterness, and wickedness from your heart, so that you deny the enemy access to your heart [7]. It means dismissing the painful issues, giving up all claims against the one who offended you, cancelling any indebtedness, making no more mention of the matter, stopping resentment and anger, and cancelling any punishment you had planned for them [7]. As Ephesians 4:32 says, we are to be kind and tenderhearted, forgiving one another even as God for Christ's sake has forgiven us [7].

It also means walking in love and praying for those who offend you, loving your enemies and blessing those who curse you [7]. And a real test of it is being able to pray sincerely for the well-being of the one who hurt you [1].

items.question: What happens spiritually to a Christian who commits fornication?
items.text:
When a Christian commits fornication, the Bible says he destroys his own soul — "he that doeth it destroyeth his own soul" (Proverbs 6:32) [1][2]. It has a real effect on you spiritually, even if you cannot say exactly how; it affects you and will lead you to backslide, and your inner self is affected [1][2]. With experience, the writer says that when somebody commits fornication his spiritual life takes a nosedive, and when a Christian falls into immorality his lifestyle changes — the destruction of the soul has begun [1][2].

It is also disobedience to God, and obedience means more to Him than any sacrifice you can make (1 Samuel 15:22) [7]. It pays to obey God, but it is very expensive to disobey Him [1][2][7]. And it is not only the soul: the one who commits fornication sins directly against his own body (1 Corinthians 6:18), and God will prosecute that crime against your body [2][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Spiritual Dangers* and chapter 3 of *All About Fornication*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:22; Proverbs 6:32; 1 Corinthians 6:15; 1 Corinthians 6:18-19.

items.question: How do I get my life ready to die?
items.text:
What a good and sober question, and our books speak to it plainly.

To set your house in order is to get ready for death and eternity, and that command is given to all of us, not only to Hezekiah [1]. One way to get ready is to prepare for the gospel and preach it for the rest of your life, because what you did with the gospel and whether you served the Lord will matter so much in eternity [1]. Preparing to preach the gospel is preparing for eternity [1].

Being ready also means being ready at any time, in season and out of season (2 Timothy 4:2), not putting God's work off to some later season of your life [3]. A strong Christian is ready to meet God at any time, and you can only be ready through the blood of Jesus who died for you [8]. The only way to die the death of a righteous person is to fulfil your ministry, so that you can say with Christ, "It is finished" [6]. And a good general prepares for the reality of death, even making a will and an escape plan for those left behind [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 11 and 12 of *The Preparation of the Gospel*, chapter 47 of *A Good General* and chapter 10 of *How you can become a strong Christian*.

Scriptures referenced: Daniel 12:3; Amos 4:12; Romans 1:15-16; 1 Thessalonians 4:16-18; 2 Timothy 4:2.

Please also speak with your shepherd or pastor today. Where a life may be at risk, contact emergency services or a medical professional now.

items.question: How do I get closer to God through apostles, prophets, pastors, teachers and evangelists?
items.text:
The books speak plainly to this: people often do not become close to God until they accept apostles, prophets, pastors, teachers and evangelists, because these are doors for you into His presence [1]. The writer says he grew closer to God by accepting great prophets and pastors into his life, and that you cannot go far without true apostles and prophets, nor get far without a pastor, a teacher or an evangelist [1]. So receive your apostle, prophet and pastor, and go through that five-pillared door into the Holy Place [1].

Be thankful for these servants too, for God's servants are God's gift to you, given as an expression of His love — as Ephesians 4:11 says, He gave gifts unto men: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers [4]. And let the Word stay central: all these offices have a primary function of teaching and preaching, and anything that does not put the Word of God in its proper place is doomed to failure with the passage of time [6][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 18 of *Steps to God's Presence*, chapter 1 of *How Can I Say Thanks*, chapter 18 of *The Art of Hearing* and chapter 11 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*.

Scriptures referenced: Luke 7:16; Ephesians 4:11-13; 1 Thessalonians 5:12.

items.question: How can I stay focused and really connect with God when I pray instead of getting distracted or falling asleep?
items.text:
What a real struggle this is, and our books speak to it directly. One key is to create an atmosphere where you can see and hear from God — the author describes checking into a silent hotel room and finding he could hardly pray, so he learned never to be anywhere without anointed music or preaching playing, saying that with a powerful anointed video playing it is as though you are part of a miracle service during your prayer time [1].

Distractions also need to be cut off deliberately: disconnect your phone, because the telephone is a favourite tool used by the devil to interrupt your prayer, and issue a "do not disturb" notice so the people you live with know when you are praying [2]. As for sleep, watching and praying is more important than fasting and praying, and watching involves staying up at night to pray; learn to overcome sleep by going to bed early so you can rise a great while before day, as Jesus did — He rose up a great while before day and spent a long time praying (Mark 1:35) [3]. Jesus even asked Peter, "What, could ye not watch with me one hour?" (Matthew 26:40) [4]. And don't be discouraged if it feels hard alone — quiet time prayer will help you develop a very personal relationship with God, and each time you expand your ability to pray alone, you are expanding your ability to chalk great achievements in prayer [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Seeing And Hearing*, chapter 10 of *Transform Your Pastoral Ministry*, chapter 3 of *Awake, O Sleeper* and chapter 8 of *The Secret*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 26:36-40; Matthew 26:42-44; Mark 1:35; Luke 6:12-13.

items.question: People are spreading lies about me in the church. How should I respond?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this. Our books speak directly to slander, and here is what they say.

Slanderers spread fear through their stories, and fear is an evil spirit — God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love and a sound mind (2 Timothy 1:7) [4]. So do not be alarmed by the false and misleading stories; God will cause you to trample over satan and his demonized slanderers, and it is only a matter of time before those slanderers burn in the very fuel they planned to use to burn down your church [4]. David's response is the model: "But I trusted in thee, O Lord: I said, Thou art my God" (Psalm 31:11-14) [4].

Remember too that a slanderer is a devil and an accuser, and one who goes about as a slanderer reveals secrets, while the trustworthy conceals a matter (Proverbs 11:13) [7]. People who fall into sin are to be helped to get up and walk again, not pushed further underground so they never rise again [7]. And touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm (Psalm 105:15) [7].

One caution from the books: it is difficult to erase from people's minds the impressions conveyed by slanderous stories, and pastors are often best at slandering other pastors [3]. So guard your own tongue in this — lay hands on your tongue, if necessary, and make sure there is no poison in it [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue* and chapter 5 of *Those Who Are Slanderers*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 31:11-14; Psalms 105:15; Proverbs 11:13; 2 Timothy 1:7.

items.question: Why do some Christians who give tithes prosper while others struggle?
items.book: Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich
items.text:
The books speak to this directly. Tithing is a seed sown in the house of God, and everyone who sows qualifies for a harvest — "they that sow in tears shall reap in joy" (Psalm 126:5) and "give, and it shall be given unto you... pressed down, and shaken together, and running over" (Luke 6:38) [3]. Tithing also fulfils the law of humility, which creates wealth, since it makes you bow before your Creator and acknowledge that you did not make it on your own [5][6].

But the books also name reasons tithing does not seem to work for some. Hidden sin can cancel the blessing, for "he that covereth his sins shall not prosper" (Proverbs 28:13) [1]. Wrong desires contradict the other principles, since you can "ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts" (James 4:2-3) [4]. Strife with the brethren blocks it, for "the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace" (James 3:18) [4]. And troubled marriages neutralize prayers, as 1 Peter 3:7 says, "that your prayers be not hindered" [1][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 14 and 22 of *Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 75:6-7; Psalms 126:5; Proverbs 28:13; Matthew 6:33; Luke 6:38; James 3:18; James 4:2-3; 1 Peter 3:7.

items.question: How can a husband help his wife stay beautiful?
items.text:
A husband's part in his wife's beauty is real, and the books speak to it plainly. A wife's beauty depends on many factors — her hair, her dressing, her make-up, even her happiness — so a wise husband invests in those factors, and you will reap what you sow [3]. Beauty also depends on money: the more you have, the more you can invest in making your wife beautiful, which is another reason a Christian husband should prosper [2]. Be concerned about which dress she wears, since her beauty depends on her dressing [2], and tell her how you like her hair and how to do it, since she desires to please you and no one else [3].

This is not vanity but love: a man is to nourish and cherish his wife as his own body, as Ephesians 5:25-29 says, and it is for his own good to nourish, cherish and beautify his wife [4]. Let her feel loved, wanted and accepted [4], and let her feel accepted and special, staying home as often as possible, not being harsh with her, as Colossians 3:19 says, and listening to her a lot [4]. Also be careful never to make scathing remarks about her body, but speak the truth in love, as Ephesians 4:15 says, loving her as your own body, as Ephesians 5:28 says [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Beauty* and chapters 11 and 32 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 5:18; Ecclesiastes 9:9; 1 Corinthians 11:15; Ephesians 4:15; Ephesians 5:25-29; Colossians 3:19.

items.question: What does the Bible say about wasting opportunities?
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this. Wasting an opportunity is a real loss — the prodigal son "wasted his substance with riotous living" (Luke 15:13), and one way people lose good opportunities is by living extravagantly, spending beyond their means [1]. He wasted the chance to benefit from his father's advice, and Judas likewise wasted the best counsel, teaching, and example he had [2].

The road to lost opportunities often begins with separation — the prodigal "took his journey into a far country," away from fellowship, because there are certain sins a believer cannot commit while walking with the brethren [3]. Greed also squanders opportunity, as it did for Gehazi (2 Kings 5:27) [6]. And we are warned that we will give an account of our stewardship, for "thou mayest be no longer steward" (Luke 16:1-2) [5].

But an opportunity is also a chance to serve the Lord, to preach the Word, and to give yourself to God's purposes [7]. So do not waste the opportunity to win souls, for "what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" (Matthew 16:26) [4], nor the blessing of the pastors God has sent to you (1 Thessalonians 5:12-13) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 4 and 10 of *Opportunities*, chapter 14 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath* and chapter 24 of *Ready@20*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Kings 5:27; Matthew 16:26; Luke 15:11-14; Luke 16:1-2; 1 Thessalonians 5:12-13.

items.question: How should a church deal with sin and rebellion among its leaders?
items.text:
Our books speak to this plainly. Sin must not be trivialized or dealt with lightly; when someone has to be dismissed, he must be dismissed, and a step of judgment, rejection, dismissal, suspension or removal must be taken, otherwise the organization will begin to decline [1]. Instead of ignoring sin and wickedness and allowing evil to grow in our midst, it must receive a stiff rejection at the highest levels [1]. At the same time, God combines judgment and restoration very well when He deals with us, so we must master the art of the official rejection of sin as well as the official pardoning of sin [1].

On rebellion specifically, you must reject rebels and have nothing to do with anyone rebelling, because if you admire a rebellious person you are in great danger of becoming a rebel yourself [2]. Rebellion is a unique sin, distinct from every other sin, and rebels are evil men who constantly defy and confront authorities [3]. God does not need you to correct His servants; God can correct His servants without you [5]. And a person who lives continually in sin is often in rebellion against God, and that attitude of rebellion can be turned unto any of God's representatives at short notice [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 79 of *The Gift Of Governments*, chapters 5 and 8 of *Those Who Rebel* and chapter 5 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

items.question: How do I stay filled with the Holy Spirit?
items.book: The Sweet Influences of the Anointing
items.text:
What a good thing to long for, pastor. Our books say a great deal about this, and the thread running through them is that being filled is something we can stir up.

Prayer meetings are one place this happens: the early church "were all filled with the Holy Ghost" after they prayed, and every prayer meeting brings down the presence of the Holy Spirit [1]. You can also stir up hunger by talking and preaching about the Holy Spirit, since "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled" (Matthew 5:6) [5], and by asking specifically for Him, since the Father gives the Holy Spirit to them that ask Him [5].

Ephesians 5:18-21 gives five keys: speaking to yourselves in psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, with melody from the heart [1][3]; giving thanks always for all things [2][3]; and submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God, which is humility [2]. Thankfulness fills you with the Spirit, while criticism and murmuring fill you with evil spirits [3][4]. And flow with Him as a real person — talk with Him, greet Him, listen for His advice [6] — for He is also like water that refreshes and makes you grow, so that you are "like a watered garden" (Isaiah 58:11) [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 31 of *The Sweet Influences of the Anointing*, chapter 3 of *Those Who Forget* and chapters 1 and 7 of *Flow in the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 63:1; Isaiah 58:11; Matthew 5:6; John 20:22; Acts 2:2; Acts 4:31; Ephesians 5:18-21; 2 Timothy 1:6.

items.question: What does the Bible say about pastors criticizing or attacking other pastors and ministries?
items.book: The Church Must Send or It Will End
items.text:
Our books speak plainly about this, and they do not approve of it. Pastors who attack and criticize one another are warned that a ministry can come to an end because of an attack on another person's ministry, and we are told to leave other ministers to God, since His judgment is greater than our criticism [2]. When pastors deride and denigrate other ministers, the question is whether they are building or destroying the Body, and we are told not to break down someone else's house or church in order to build our own, for you will reap what you sow [4].

The books also describe this as a danger sign: attacking and killing your own brother is a very bad sign, and constant analysis, criticism and mockery of fellow ministers is common in the conversation of some pastors [3]. We are told we shall know them by their fruits, and when the fruits are broken churches, destroyed ministries and deceived pastors, the Spirit of God is not at work [1]. One passage goes further and says you must reject rebels and abhor those in rebellion, citing Psalm 139:21 [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 5 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*, chapter 4 of *The Church Must Send or It Will End*, chapter 8 of *Those who are Dangerous Sons* and chapter 8 of *Those Who Rebel*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 4:8-12; Joshua 22:19; 2 Samuel 13:28; 2 Samuel 14:28; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalms 139:21.

items.question: A leader I trained for years has just left the church. How do I handle it?
items.text:
I'm sorry — that kind of departure cuts deep, especially after years of investing in someone. Let me share what our books say.

First, guard your own spirit. The event of someone leaving has an effect on you; leavers pollute your spirit with seeds of hurt, anger, hatred, wickedness and revenge, and you will need to pray long and hard to get free from them, lest you fall into bitterness and unforgiveness [4]. And be careful how you judge the reasons — those who mocked another church's "bad leader" later had the very thing happen to them, more severely [3].

On the practical side, the books say to remove disloyal people quickly: if someone indicates a desire to leave, it is best for them not to stay but to go immediately, because their heart has already left, and "a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6) [7]. Jesus told Judas, "That thou doest, do quickly" (John 13:27) [7]. A disloyal assistant left with almost a whole church of three thousand, reducing it to twenty, so such people must be handled with knowledge and God's wisdom, and a "Judas" is to be restricted rather than left free to operate normally [2].

There is also hope here. Sometimes the departure of a person heralds the arrival of God's choice for you — it was when Saul's heart departed that David was revealed [6]. If you are open, each person who leaves can become a stepping stone to a higher dimension of ministry [5]. And it is worth asking honestly whether the Lord allowed this because you have not continued to follow Him as at the beginning, or because you have not exerted your authority [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 33 of *Victory Secrets*, chapters 1 and 10 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 3 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 11:3-4; Psalms 141:9-10; Proverbs 3:7; John 13:27; 1 Corinthians 5:6; 1 Corinthians 14:33; 2 Corinthians 7:11.

items.question: How can a pastor's wife support her husband's ministry if she's quiet and doesn't connect with people?
items.book: The Beauty The Beast and The Pastor
items.text:
The books speak directly to this. A wife who is helpful is a quiet and effective backbone to any minister, and many ministers depend on their wives for the quiet and effective help they give [2]. That help is pictured as the salt of the earth — quiet and effective, working behind the scenes, like the helps ministry of prayer warriors, secretaries, or others not seen or known by the general public [1][2]. So being quiet is not the opposite of supporting him; it is one of the ways the books describe that support.

But the books also warn strongly against isolation. To be non-communicative is a serious flaw in your ministry, and to be isolated is a serious mistake; those who are non-communicative rarely do well, and isolation is said to kill your potential [5]. We need each other, and speaking and communicating will drive away demons from your life and ministry [5]. So the books hold both: a quiet, behind-the-scenes helper [1][2], and a warning that isolation and non-communication are serious flaws [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *Am I Good For Nothing?* and chapter 4 of *Why Is This Church Not Working?*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 2:18; Matthew 6:3-4; Romans 12:8; 1 Corinthians 12:20-21; 1 Corinthians 12:28; Hebrews 11:40.

items.question: How should I respond when people I've loved and helped turn against me?
items.text:
Friend, this is a pain every shepherd comes to know, and our books speak to it plainly.

Don't be surprised by it. Jesus Himself experienced ingratitude — He was killed by an ungrateful mob, exchanged for an armed robber, yet never responded to that evil spirit [1]. Every leader comes face to face with ingratitude, and people are not grateful for the services you render them [1]. Some of the people the author loved returned his love with flatness, with hatred, with treachery [5], and wicked men say "thank you" for your love by becoming your adversaries, as Psalm 109 says, "For my love they are my adversaries: but I give myself unto prayer" [4].

So do not look to people for gratitude — a leader looks to God for rewards, for "whatsoever good thing any man doeth, the same shall he receive of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:8) [1]. Do not let offences turn you away from your mission; Jesus was not turned away by the hurts and offences of ministry, and you must learn to forgive because you have been forgiven a lot [8]. Do not struggle when people are taken away from you — sometimes it is in your eternal destiny that they be taken away and replaced, and the departure of a person can herald the arrival of God's choice for you [6][7].

One caution: the books also record David's response of praying down judgment on those who repaid his good with evil, asking God to clothe them with shame and dishonour (Psalm 35, Psalm 109) [2][3]. The passages set both before you — Jesus' silence and forgiveness [1][8], and David's cry for God's judgment [2][3] — without telling you which to choose.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 101 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 3 of *How Can I Say Thanks*, chapter 11 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*, chapters 1 and 10 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 5 of *Why Few Are Chosen*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 18:1-2; Psalms 35:21-26; Psalms 109:1-13; Luke 15:11-13; John 10:32; John 21:15-17; Ephesians 6:8; 1 John 2:18-19.

items.question: What does the cross mean for me as a Christian?
items.text:
The cross is the true symbol of Christianity, and every time you see it you are meant to be reminded of what it stands for [3]. It is first of all the symbol of death you must experience: a person carrying a cross was on his way to die, so when Jesus said to take up your cross daily and follow Him (Luke 9:23), He was telling you to go to a place where you lose your life, because Christianity is about dying so that you may live a new life in Christ [4].

It is also the symbol of the price you must pay, for you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:20) [1]; the symbol of the love of God you must emulate, since He laid down His life for us and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren (1 John 3:16) [1]; the symbol of obedience, for Christ humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross (Philippians 2:8) [1][5]; and the symbol of the sacrifice all of us must make to serve the Lord, as Christ gave Himself for us as an offering and a sacrifice to God (Ephesians 5:2) [1][5]. In the cross Jesus humbled Himself to the uttermost and made Himself of no reputation [5], and it is the symbol of His blood, for through the blood of His cross He reconciled all things to Himself (Colossians 1:20) [5].

Taking up your cross also releases power in your life: it puts away sins, for when someone makes great sacrifices his flaws seem to fade away [6], and it enables you to die to sin and live to righteousness [6]. It is the power by which separation from the world takes place, so that you will not mind being the odd one out, or being a virgin when others are not, or giving up wealth to pursue the ministry [2]. And a cross takes away the curse due rebellious people, for Christ was made a curse for us, as it is written, "Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree" (Galatians 3:13) [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 15 and 17 of *Losing, Suffering, Sacrificing and Dying*.

Scriptures referenced: Luke 9:23; 1 Corinthians 6:20; Galatians 3:13; Ephesians 5:2; Philippians 2:8; Colossians 1:20; Hebrews 2:9; Hebrews 9:24-26; 1 John 3:16.

items.question: How do I stop needing people's approval and praise after I preach?
items.text:
What a good and freeing question. The books speak to this directly.

Do not look to people for gratitude or approval; a leader looks to God for rewards, for "whatsoever good thing any man doeth, the same shall he receive of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:8) [1]. Your rewards depend on God, not on the people you helped, so expect your rewards from God rather than from men [1]. One pastor described how he stopped expecting people to commend him after preaching, and when he decided not to look for man's approval he felt a sense of liberty, free from men and accountable to the Lord [1].

The same counsel appears elsewhere: you do not need the approval of men, so do not worry about what people think of you — just make sure God thinks highly of you, and you will become a workman who is not ashamed (2 Timothy 2:15-16) [2]. People may congratulate you, but it is the Lord's approval you really need [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 101 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 9 of *The Preparation of the Gospel* and chapter 2 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: John 3:16; John 10:32; Ephesians 6:8; 2 Timothy 2:15-16; 2 Timothy 4:1-2.

items.question: How can I learn to pray early in the morning before my day gets busy?
items.book:
Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer
items.text:
What a good desire, pastor. The books speak directly to this. Jesus Himself rose "a great while before day" and went to a solitary place to pray (Mark 1:35), and you are invited to learn how to do the same [1]. One practical step they give is to go to bed early so that you can rise a great while before day — that was the life of Jesus [3].

They also frame it as a habit worth building: praying at dawn is very repeatable, something you can do tomorrow and every day of the year, even on your busiest days [1]. And they warn that life in the secular world is not designed to include a prayer time, so you must deliberately include it [5][7]. If you decide to develop a habit of prayer, you are developing a habit for success [5][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*, chapter 3 of *Awake, O Sleeper*, chapter 1 of *How to Pray* and chapter 8 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*.

Scriptures referenced: Daniel 6:10; Matthew 26:36-40; Mark 1:34-36; Luke 4:16.

items.question: How can I pray for the sick and be a source of healing?
items.text:
You can become a source of healing by praying for the sick, because healing is on the heart of God and Jesus said He was anointed to heal the broken-hearted (Luke 4:18) [1]. Many people are comforted when hands are laid on them, so believe in the ministry of healing—it is a real ministry [1].

Don't run from the opportunity to pray for the sick; every testimony, even of headaches healed, is a rehearsal for greater days ahead, and Jesus Himself sent His disciples out to cure diseases and heal the sick (Luke 9:1-2) [2]. Keep your prayers short, as Jesus did—He prayed briefly for the sick, saying "Ephphatha, that is, be opened" (Mark 7:34-35) [3]. And expect fear to come, for fear is a spirit that keeps you from using your gifts; the author describes overcoming that fear as his greatest barrier to this ministry [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *Am I Good For Nothing?*, chapter 2 of *The Preparation of the Gospel*, chapter 17 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer* and chapter 15 of *Many Are Called*.

Scriptures referenced: Mark 7:34-35; Luke 4:18; Luke 9:1-2; Luke 23:34; John 6:11; John 11:41-42.

items.question: How can I know my strengths and use them for God?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly. God has asked you to be strong in the grace He has given you, and whatever grace He has given you, you should flow in it [1]. Knowing your temperament — choleric, sanguine, melancholic or phlegmatic — will help you know your strengths and flow in them [1]. For example, the phlegmatic has a grace to do the same thing repeatedly and to carry on in monotonous tasks, so be a good teacher, pastor or headmaster and flow in it [1]; the melancholic has a grace to be talented, deep-thinking and faithful, so flow in your God-given gift [1][2]; the choleric has strength to be a driving personality, a finisher of projects and a natural manager, so walk in that strength of leadership [2]; and the sanguine has grace to be cheerful, happy and pleasant at all times, so do not despise this great strength [2].

A true leader knows where his strength lies, and when you discover your strengths, flow in them [2][3]. Do not be a pastor because everyone is pastoring a church, or a prophet because it is the latest fad; stay in the area which makes you unique, develop it and become strong [3]. items.question: How do I know my work for God is not a waste of time?
items.text:
Your labour in the Lord is not in vain — Paul said so plainly: "be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord" [2]. Solomon called his own work vanity, but Paul described his work differently [2]. So the assurance isn't that the work will feel easy, but that work done in the Lord is not empty.

You'll also know it by what it does in you. When you find your life's work, money no longer drives you; you work for the joy of fulfilling God's will, saying with Jesus, "My meat is to do the will of him that sent me" [1][2]. And doing the work helps you overcome your personal problems — as we minister the Word, our difficulties become smaller, for we have "this treasure in earthen vessels" (2 Corinthians 4:7) [3]. If you're tired, that's only a sign the activity has entered the realm of work [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *Rules of Church Work (2nd Edition)*, chapter 2 of *Church Planting* and chapter 10 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 20:11; Nehemiah 4:6; Esther 4:14; Proverbs 6:10-11; Ecclesiastes 3:13; Ecclesiastes 5:10; Ecclesiastes 5:19; Matthew 6:20; Luke 12:15; John 9:4 and 2 more.

items.question: How can I motivate the people who follow me as a leader?
items.text:
What a good question to be asking, pastor. The books speak to this in several ways.

First, be yourself and speak from your heart. People love to hear leaders speaking naturally from their hearts rather than reading boring speeches, and no one wants to follow a pretender [2]. A leader must recognize the emotional nature of human beings and speak in a way that inspires people to follow, putting away lifeless speeches and speaking from the heart [3]. You cannot motivate people if you yourself are not motivated [3].

Second, go first. The master key to leading people anywhere is to walk the road yourself; Jesus never told his disciples to do things that he himself did not do [4]. You cannot get people to pray if you do not pray yourself [2]. Convince people to go anywhere by going first [4].

Third, give them a future and a hope. A true leader wants the people he is leading to become great, and when they feel that in following you they will become great, they will be very willing to stay close [1]. Sacrifice to make them happy, and aim for your followers to do well spiritually and financially [1][7]. Julius Caesar boosted the morale of his troops by promising them land when they returned home [8].

And fourth, speak to your people. Leaders who do not speak to their troops fail to raise the morale of their troops; you must rise up and speak to your people, encourage them, and tell them that it will be well [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 16, 79, 83, 91 and 92 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 9 of *A Good General*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 26:35; Mark 1:17; John 14:12; Acts 3:6; Acts 20:33-37; 3 John 4.

items.question: What does the Bible say happens to a society that stops being thankful to God?
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this. When people knew God but did not glorify Him or give thanks, they became vain in their imaginations and their foolish hearts were darkened, and professing themselves wise they became fools (Romans 1:21) [2][3]. Because of this unthankfulness, God gave them up — to uncleanness, to vile affections, and to dishonoring their own bodies, with men and women turning from the natural use one toward another (Romans 1:26-28) [1][3].

The books describe the result as a descent into total perversion, total foolishness, total madness and total destruction, and say the human race is teetering on the brink of destruction because of our ungratefulness [3]. Unthankfulness is listed among the terrible faults of the last days, when men will be more and more ungrateful (2 Timothy 3:1-5) [6]. It is also called a dangerous curse that opens a person up to wicked spirits [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *How Can I Say Thanks* and chapter 7 of *Pillars of Loyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Judges 9:16-21; Romans 1:21; Romans 1:26-28; Colossians 3:15; 1 Timothy 4:3-5; 2 Timothy 3:1-5.

items.question: How do I know if I've been called by God to do His work?
items.text:
What a good and weighty question, pastor. Our books speak to this in several ways.

One sign the books point to is a supernatural desire for the work. Paul asked Timothy to look for the desire and didn't even mention the call, because the desire is a manifestation of a divine call [4]. The desire for ministry is a symptom of a divine call within, a burden put there by God [6]. Paul himself had a heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel, that they might be saved (Romans 10:1), and that desire was translated into practical ministry time and time again [6].

The books also say you must be sure you are called, and not call yourself, since no man can take this honour unto himself (Hebrews 5:4) [2]. Ministry must wait until there is a definite call [2]. And your call is specific — a commission that only you can accomplish, as no one in the Bible had the commission Jonah had [2]. You are also destined to be called; the call of God is no accident, and those who believe they are called take God's Word, their dreams, their visions, and their quiet times more seriously [7].

One caution: the books note that many people don't even know what it means to have a divine call, and don't know whether they are called or not [6]. So look for that genuine desire, and be sure of the call before you step in.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry*, chapter 3 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd* and chapter 2 of *Predestination*.

Scriptures referenced: Romans 8:30; Romans 10:1; 1 Timothy 4:15; Hebrews 5:4.

items.question: How do I forgive someone who hurt me very badly?
items.text:
I'm sorry you've been hurt so badly. The books speak directly to this. One step is to analyse the offender — Jesus prayed, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34), and often the person who hurts us is not fully aware of what they are doing; making excuses for them, as Jesus did for His own murderers, helps us forgive [2][5]. Another step is to analyse your own past sins and consider yourself, lest you also be tempted [5].

Forgiveness itself means dismissing the thorny, painful issues, giving up all claims against the one who offended you, cancelling any indebtedness, making no more mention of the matter, stopping resentment and anger, and cancelling all punishments you have planned [1][3]. It also means walking in love and praying for your offender, as Matthew 5 teaches about loving your enemies and praying for those who despitefully use you [1]. And remember, you are equally in need of forgiveness from God, for if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you (Matthew 6:14) [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 18 of *Those Who Are Offended* and chapter 5 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 6:14; Luke 23:34; Ephesians 4:32; Hebrews 12:3.

items.question: A member has stopped coming to church and stopped praying. How do I help them come back to God?
items.text:
Our books speak to this. Staying in fellowship matters: if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship one with another (1 John 1:7), and if you are in the light you will go to church and fellowship with other Christians [3]. A Christian who doesn't pray is a Christian who will fall into one temptation after another until he eventually backslides, and an uncommitted Christian is a potential backslider [8]. God expects the believer to be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, planted in the house of the Lord, with somebody to relate to as pastor — you need to belong somewhere [8].

So keep the door open and keep praying. It is time to come back home, and staying in fellowship is an important key to receiving the blessings of the Lord [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *How to Pray* and chapter 7 of *Backsliding*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 119:133; Proverbs 7:10; 1 John 1:7; 1 John 3:22.

items.question: What happens in my life when I don't pray?
items.text:
When you do not pray, your life is directed by happenstance—what looks like chance, luck, or fate is often governed by natural and spiritual forces, not random coincidence [1]. Ahab's death, for instance, looked like a random arrow, but it was orchestrated by evil spirits [2].

Without prayer, your life is also governed by the major curses in this world—the curse on Adam, the curse on Eve, and the curse on Ham—and by the god of this world, Satan, who directs the affairs of the earth into wars, conflicts, and sorrows [2][7]. Human beings will also take decisions that affect you; if you do not pray, the will of capricious and unreasonable men will be implemented in your life [3]. And when you do not pray, you do not intervene or modify events taking place in the spirit realm, where spiritual events trigger things in the natural [5].

The remedy the books give is prayer, especially for wisdom, which delivers you from these patterns and curses [4][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *How to Pray* and chapter 2 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 22:30-35; Proverbs 3:13-16; 2 Corinthians 4:4.

items.question: How can a young person stay away from sexual sin?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and gently. First, respect your sexuality rather than denying it — a proper respect for youthful lusts, rather than a denial of them, will save you from them [3]. And know that God's will is clear here: "For this is the will of God, your sanctification; that you abstain from sexual immorality" (1 Thessalonians 4:3-4), so make sexual purity one of your clearest and most energetic goals [2].

Practically, the books give steps. Do not enter into relationships at the wrong time — very young people should not enter into courtship, for "to every thing there is a season" (Ecclesiastes 3:1) [5]. Enter only into relationships that lead to marriage, since the only intimate relationship God approves of is marriage [5]. Stay away from anyone who would want such a relationship with you, and find your own way of keeping yourself from fornication — it may be God's will for you to avoid certain books or films, certain friends, or certain places [2]. And be visible rather than hidden: sit in the front, make sure your pastor knows your name, for those who sit far away are often practicing some kind of evil [8].

There is also hope here, not only warning. Holiness is engineered by the Spirit of holiness, not by being older — age has nothing to do with holiness, and every young person can be empowered by the Spirit of holiness [7]. God promises, "I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes" (Ezekiel 36:27), so young people can live free from sin [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing*, chapters 10, 13 and 24 of *Ready@20* and chapter 4 of *Spiritual Dangers*.

items.question: How do I know if I'm ready to step into a bigger role in ministry?
items.text:
Friend, our books speak to this. They say readiness is not something you settle by reading about it, but by doing the will of God — as John 7:17 says, if anyone is willing to do His will, he will know the teaching [2]. The books also say God does not put inexperienced people into the ministry; you need experience to be effective, and Scripture warns that an overseer must not be a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil (1 Timothy 3:6) [4].

They also describe a line of service with four levels — doing the work, having a gift, having a ministry, and occupying an office — and note that when several people are helping and serving under you, it is often a sign that you are occupying a spiritual office [4]. And they counsel wisdom about timing: many ministries are frustrated because people entered full-time ministry too quickly, and success requires both power and wisdom, as 1 Corinthians 1:24 says [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)*, chapter 14 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd* and chapter 15 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: John 7:17; Romans 11:13; Romans 12:6; 1 Corinthians 1:24; 1 Timothy 3:6; 2 Timothy 4:5.

items.question: Why is the shepherd's ministry so important in the church?
items.text:
The shepherd's ministry matters because it is the shepherd, not the prophet, whose absence scatters the sheep; God promises to set up shepherds who will save His people, and it is through the shepherd that the earth yields her increase and the people dwell safely [1]. The prophet Ezekiel declares this, and the ministry of the shepherd is prophetically destined to change the landscape of the church [1].

It is also a principal duty of the shepherd to feed the sheep, and the authority to lead is given to those with the ability to feed [2]. Jesus said to Peter three times, "Feed my sheep" (John 21:17), showing how important it is to the Lord that His sheep are well fed on the Word of God [2]. Alongside this, one of the principal ministries of a shepherd is to comfort the sheep, so that every sheep can say, "Your rod and your staff comfort me" (Psalm 23:4) [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *The Double Mega Missionary Church* and chapter 11 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 23:4; Proverbs 22:10; Micah 7:14; Mark 6:46; Luke 5:15-16; John 21:17.

items.question: What habits did Jesus have that made Him great?
items.text:
Jesus had a habit of going to church regularly — the Bible says He went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, "as his custom was" (Luke 4:16) [1][2][3]. He also had a habit of going on prayer retreats; He often went to a particular garden, and everyone knew His habit of praying there, for "Jesus ofttimes resorted thither with his disciples" (John 18:1-2) [1][2][3].

The books also hold up Daniel, who prayed at specific times of the day — three times a day, as he did aforetime (Daniel 6:10) — and say this was one of the greatest secrets of his life [1][2][3].

items.question: How can I show God that I'm thankful for everything He's done for me?
items.text:
What a good question to ask, pastor. The books say the only real way to say "thank you" to Jesus is with your life — not just with songs or words you've learned, since those aren't your own [5]. He gave you Himself, so you give Him yourself, and that becomes a reasonable service, a reasonable sacrifice, a reasonable ministry [5].

Practically, that means presenting your body as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service, and being transformed by the renewing of your mind rather than conformed to this world, as Romans 12:1-2 says [2][4]. It also means labouring more abundantly than everyone else, as Paul put it in 1 Corinthians 15:10 — working harder because you're conscious of the grace shown to you [2]. And it means being willing, fast and complete in your obedience, showing your gratefulness that God called you, as Romans 8:29-30 says [3].

And be careful to avoid unthankfulness, since 2 Timothy 3:2 lists it among the serious evils of the last days [7].

items.question: Where do demons come from?
items.text:
The books say demons are not the same as fallen angels or Satan; they are a separate set of creatures, called *diamonion* in the Greek, while the devil comes from *diabolos* [1][2]. They came about through the fallen angels' invasion of human beings: the hybrid "para-human" offspring of angels and women died, and their half-human, half-angel spirits were confined to the earth and roam about as demons [1][2]. As Enoch 15:8-10 puts it, "the giants, who are produced from the spirits and flesh, shall be called evil spirits on the earth" [2].

The books also describe another origin for unclean animal spirits: fallen angels had intercourse with animals, and the offspring of those unions continued to interbreed, producing the wicked spirit-animal creatures known as unclean spirits [4]. And God did not set out to create evil; He saw all He had made and it was very good (Genesis 1:31), yet He gave the angels free will, which is why some were able to rebel [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 15 and 17 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies* and chapter 4 of *One of You is a Devil*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 1:31; Colossians 1:16; Jude 6.

items.question: How can I become a friend of God like Abraham was?
items.text:
What a good thing to long for. Our books say that Abraham was called a friend of God, and they point to obedience as the heart of it: he passed the test of obedience, which is the test of love, when he was willing to sacrifice his son [4]. Being a friend of God is not just a cliché; it is a real thing, and Abraham was completely sold out to God, with no third party coming between him and God [2].

They also tie this friendship to sacrifice: Abraham became a friend of God by being willing to sacrifice his only son (Genesis 22:16, James 2:23) [3]. And they warn that anything that becomes too precious will attract the Lord's attention, for our God is a jealous God who hates the very smell of idols [5]. So the picture given is a life of obeying God no matter what it costs, holding nothing back from Him [2][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 11 of *If You Love The Lord*, chapter 12 of *One Thousand Micro Churches* and chapter 5 of *The Art of Following*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 22:16-17; Deuteronomy 13:1-3; Isaiah 41:8; Daniel 8:11-13; John 12:24; Romans 12:1-2; 2 Corinthians 8:24; James 2:23; 1 John 5:21.

items.question: How should I keep the Sabbath day as a Christian?
items.text:
The books speak to this plainly. The Sabbath is a day for going to church and hearing the word of God — Jesus went to the synagogue on the Sabbath as His custom, and Paul and Barnabas went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day [1][7]. It is God-time, not family time, and not a day for football, golf, washing, or visiting friends [1][6]. It is also a day of rest from secular work, and you need not worry about which day of the week it is — there must simply be a day you have chosen to set apart for God [7]. Keeping it is a sign that sets God's people apart, and it tests your willingness to be holy, special, and obedient [3][8].

At the same time, the books also say it is lawful to do well on the Sabbath day, and that the donkey was considered worthy of deliverance and healing on the Sabbath — so how much more a human being [2]. Jesus asked, "Is it lawful to do well on the Sabbath day?" (Luke 14:3), and Matthew 12:12 says it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days [2]. The books also warn against being bound by traditions that do not follow the most basic laws of common sense, fairness and logic, and urge you to let the Holy Spirit guide you away from such traditions [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Seven Great Principles*, chapter 25 of *Stir It Up* and chapter 4 of *WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 16:23; Exodus 31:12-17; Exodus 35:2; Leviticus 23:27-32; Ezekiel 20:21; Malachi 3:10; Matthew 12:12; Mark 1:21; Luke 14:3; Acts 13:14-16 and 1 more.

items.question: How can I have a closer relationship with God?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and the heart of it is drawing near to God personally, not just publicly. As James 4:8 says, "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you" [1][3][5][7]. Knowing about God from afar is different from knowing Him personally, and that personal relationship is not developed at church services, conventions, or crusades, but through a daily quiet time of personal interaction with Him [1][5][7]. It is up to you to draw near to Him on a daily basis, rather than expecting Him to come to you [3][7].

When you are alone with someone, you become close and intimate, and you develop a bond and a knowledge you cannot acquire in public [8]. As Paul prayed, "That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection" (Philippians 3:10) [8]. One caution the books give: as you get closer to God you may sense your own unworthiness and sin, and to love Him properly you must overcome that inferiority by accepting that you are forgiven and that the past is washed away by the blood of Jesus [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapter 6 of *Attempt Great Things for God*, chapter 5 of *The Secret* and chapter 21 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 27:33-36; Ephesians 4:3; Philippians 3:10; James 4:8; 1 John 1:1-2.

items.question: How can a husband and wife make love in a way that is enjoyable for both of them?
items.text:
What a good thing to want for each other. Your books say sex was created by God as something beautiful and pleasurable to be enjoyed by both husband and wife, not just for procreation [1], and that it is an art to be learned and developed, about having fun with your partner and showing care rather than scoring 10 out of 10 for performance [5].

So decide together to make it pleasurable, with both of you setting out to give and derive maximum excitement [1]. Be nice to each other during the day with small thoughtful acts, look nice, smell nice and be clean, and choose a place and lighting that suit you both [1]. Let foreplay begin with endearing conversation, loving pats, hugs and kisses [1], and keep stimulating each other during the act by holding tightly, caressing and kissing [4]. Talk to each other and express your feelings during the act, and let your partner know which movements stimulate you or distract you [1][4]. Remember that a woman's arousal builds slowly, like an electric iron heating up, while a man's is like a light switched on [1][4] — so the husband should continue kissing and caressing her until she is sexually excited [1]. Tell each other when you feel you are reaching orgasm, and let your partner feel that he or she has done something wonderful to you [4]. You may also repeat the whole process as many times as there is strength, since multiple orgasms and ejaculations are possible [4].

The books also encourage you to be adventurous and create variety, not holding yourselves back, and to abandon yourselves totally into each other's arms [8]. Kissing is an important form of intimacy, as Song of Solomon 1:2 says, and it is exciting whilst making love — beware of letting it fade out of your marriage [3]. And as Proverbs 5:19 says, let her breasts satisfy thee at all times, and be thou ravished always with her love: satisfy each other at all times, and make a conscious effort to admire the different parts of your spouse's body and beauty [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 28, 31, 33 and 38 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 5:19; Song of Songs 1:2.

items.question: How can I pray like Jesus did?
items.text:
What a good thing to want, pastor. Our books hold up Jesus' own prayer life as the pattern.

There are times to pray short and powerful prayers, as Jesus did at Lazarus' tomb, believing God has heard you and then acting boldly [1][5]. But there are also times to spend long hours in prayer — Jesus went out to a mountain and continued all night in prayer to God (Luke 6:12), and rose a great while before day to pray in a solitary place (Mark 1:35) [1][5]. You can stay on the same topic for hours; it is not useless repetition, it is praying like Jesus did [1][2][3]. Start with one hour and graduate to three, then five and seven [1][5]. Jesus prayed three hours in Gethsemane and was surprised the disciples could not watch with Him one hour (Matthew 26:40) [4].

He also prayed with strong crying and tears, as Hebrews 5:7 says, and was heard — though that is a dimension, not a demand to always shout [2][3]. And He gave thanks: "Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me" (John 11:41-42) [1][5], for in everything God wants us to give thanks (1 Thessalonians 5:18) [2][3]. One more thing — He prayed only what He saw the Father doing (John 5:19), praying according to His will (1 John 5:14) [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *100% Answered Prayer* and chapters 1, 7 and 9 of *How to Pray*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 26:39-40; Matthew 26:42-44; Mark 1:35; Luke 6:12; John 5:19; John 11:41-42; 1 Thessalonians 5:18; Hebrews 5:7; 1 John 5:14.

items.question: How can my wife and I build a strong marriage?
items.text:
What a good thing to be asking. The books say a happy home does not just happen; it must be developed, and nothing happens by chance [7]. Christ must be acknowledged as the foundation and head of the home, for the one who hears His sayings and does them is like a man who laid his foundation on a rock, as Luke 6:47-48 says [7]. When God is the focus of both husband and wife, they draw closer to each other because their closeness to God draws them together [7].

Build your marriage around the church, attending services and being involved in church activities, and while in church, husband and wife must sit together [2][3]. Develop family worship, holding regular quiet times together or, when that is not possible, each doing it regularly, but by all means finding time to do it together, especially with the children [2][3]. Think as a Christian spouse: do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit, but in humility consider others better than yourselves, as Philippians 2:3 says, reconciling the plans you held individually before marriage to suit the home, being willing to give up certain interests and preferences for its sake, and not always insisting on your own way [3]. And speak to one another — speaking the truth in love makes us grow up in Christ, as Ephesians 4:15 says, and a husband and wife must be the best of friends, sharing every success, disappointment, joy and pain together [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 7 and 9 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Job 32:17-20; Psalms 1:1-6; Proverbs 14:4; Proverbs 18:21; Proverbs 24:3; Luke 6:47-48; Ephesians 4:15; Philippians 2:3.

items.question: What does it mean if God rewards my faithfulness with more work instead of rest?
items.book: WOM15. The Reward for Hard Work is More Work
items.text:
It means God is treating your faithfulness as a qualification for greater trust. The reward for being faithful with small things is to be given bigger things to work on [5], and the reward for working well with what belongs to another is to be given your own [1]. So more work is not a punishment but a sign of God's gratitude and confidence in you.

The books do hold out rest as a reward too — "they may rest from their labours" (Revelation 14:12-13) [2] — but they also say plainly that God does not only give rest, He gives more work after the period of rest [2]. So do not expect holidays and restful seasons; expect more hard work [4], and keep pressing on rather than thinking of retiring [3][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 5 and 8 of *WOM15. The Reward for Hard Work is More Work*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 16:27; Luke 16:10-12; 1 Timothy 5:17-18; Hebrews 11:6.
