items.question: How can I grow and be more successful without becoming overconfident and setting myself up for a fall?
items.text:
What a good and sober question. The books speak directly to it.

Growth and success are real gifts, but the danger is that pride grows alongside them. Overconfidence is one of the marks of the pride of a novice, and at its end stage every sin gets complicated by pride [1]. If you regard yourself or your position in Christ as foolproof, you are in danger of backsliding — especially if you have had promotion in church or have been used by God in the past [2]. Where you are over-confident is where you can be the weakest, because you have dropped your guard [2].

The safeguard the books hold out is humility, which keeps you able to learn. Ministers of the gospel stop learning at the rate at which they become proud, and many ministries plateau because pride has taken away childlikeness and the ability to learn anything new [3]. When you are humble like a child, you copy things easily; when you lose that humility, you do not want to copy, even if it is a good thing [3]. Staying on the right track is largely by the grace of God, not by your own strength [2]. And be careful how you speak of others' weaknesses — criticizing others as though you could never make the same mistakes is itself a sign of overconfidence [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Not A Novice*, chapter 5 of *Backsliding* and chapter 2 of *Those who are Proud*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 16:1-4; 1 Corinthians 10:12.

items.question: How can I know the real number of people attending our church instead of just guessing?
items.text:
What you're describing is exactly what the books call Type 1 Counting—counting the heads who are actually present, which the author says is the number to stay with because "there can be no variation in the method of counting heads who are actually present" [8]. He warns against the other kinds of counting: rough estimates [1], using the seating capacity of the building as an assumption [8], and cumulative convention counts that can be misleading [8]. He also says the Sunday attendance is the best number for monitoring progress in a general way, though it is only a percentage of your true membership because attendance fluctuates [4].

He also urges you to register your members with a simple form, keeping the most important fields as names, ages, gender, telephone numbers and addresses [6], and to keep other important numbers constantly before you—weekday service attendance, small group meetings, fasting and prayer sessions, and the number absent at each service [4][7]. His reason is that the truth will tell you where you are and where you are not, and knowing the actual number of souls you minister to will motivate you to work harder [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *The Mega Church*, chapter 45 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 13 of *Church Growth*.

Scriptures referenced: Luke 13:23; John 8:32.

items.question: There is a woman in our church who manipulates and controls people. How do I deal with her?
items.book: Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order
items.text:
Our books speak directly to this. A Jezebel must not be allowed to operate freely in the church, and it angers God when she is left unchecked [7]. It takes the collective rebuke of church leadership to deal with a Jezebel; one person identifying her and crying foul is not going to correct or control her [3]. God wants more people to identify the Jezebels in our midst and stop them [3].

Many pastors are too dignified and self-righteous to confront a pastor's wife or bring her to order, and many want to maintain good relations with everybody, so they will not rebuke and correct wives who are out of order [7]. But if a Jezebel is allowed to go uncorrected, you may lose everything, just as Elijah lost his ministry [7]. One man of God confessed that the greatest mistake of his life was that they did not confront the woman; they should have stepped in and stopped the Jezebel in her tracks, and because they failed, it cost them everything [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 4 and 21 of *Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order* and chapter 15 of *Can’t You Do
Just a Little Bit More?*.

Scriptures referenced: Revelation 2:20.

items.question: What will heaven and the new earth be like?
items.book: Who Is He That Overcometh the World
items.text:
What a hope we have, pastor. The books describe a new heaven and a new earth where the first heaven and first earth have passed away, and there is no more sea [1][2]. God Himself will dwell with His people, and He will wipe away all tears from their eyes; there will be no more death, sorrow, crying, or pain, for the former things are passed away [1][3]. There will be no more curse, and the throne of God and of the Lamb will be there, and His servants shall serve Him [3][4][5].

It is also described as a very beautiful city, the New Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband [1][4]. In that city there is a pure river of water of life and a tree of life bearing twelve kinds of fruit, whose leaves are for the healing of the nations [4][5]. No evil thing, no abomination, and no liar can enter it, and there will be no night there, nor any need of a candle or the sun [4]. The kingdoms of this world will become the kingdoms of our Lord and of His Christ, and He shall reign for ever and ever [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Who Is He That Overcometh the World*, chapter 31 of *Victory Secrets* and chapter 20 of *How To Neutralize Curses*.

Scriptures referenced: Luke 4:6; Ephesians 1:21; 1 John 2:17; Revelation 11:15; Revelation 21:1-5; Revelation 22:1-5.

items.question: How can churches grow in poor areas if they can't afford to pay pastors and workers?
items.book: Laikos Lay People and the Ministry
items.text:
The books speak directly to this. The key is the lay or tent ministry — the sacrifice of pastors and evangelists who labour without being paid for their services. Without this strategy, very few churches will be planted, because it is virtually impossible for the church to employ all the people needed for the work of God [1][2]. Most of the ripened harvest fields are in the poor regions of the world, and most of those people cannot pay for the services of good pastors and evangelists, so the ministry of unpaid pastors and evangelists is the key to continued church planting [1][2].

The practical counsel is to get a job and pastor the church on the side until it grows and demands your full attention [4]. Paul himself was a tent maker, and he stayed with Aquila and Priscilla and worked together with them [1][2]. The Swiss missionaries sent to Ghana came as self-sustaining ministers, equipped with skills to work as they did their ministry [4]. And when people see that you are not ministering for financial gain, they will be more interested in your new church [5][6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry*, chapters 9 and 20 of *Church Planting*, chapter 6 of *Church Growth* and chapter 7 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Thessalonians 3:11; 1 Timothy 5:13.

items.question: What does it mean to be called by God?
items.text:
To be called by God is to be summoned distinctly — identified, called out by name, and selected by God. In Hebrew the word is *qara*, meaning to call out and properly address by name those who are bidden; in Greek it is *kletos*, meaning to be invited or appointed. Moses, Bezaleel, Samuel, Zacchaeus, and many of the disciples were called out by name [1].

It also means you have been separated for His purposes — detached from the larger group and set apart for God, as He separated the tribe of Levi to bear the ark and minister before Him (Deuteronomy 10:8) [2][7]. Your calling is according to His own purpose and grace, given us in Christ Jesus before the world began (2 Timothy 1:9), so it matters not only to obey the call but to seek out the purpose within it [6]. And it means you have received an office from the Lord, a position with special responsibilities and authority [3], along with a gift and a ministry — a natural capacity freely given, so that those called seem to do certain things effortlessly [4][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Many Are Called* and chapter 1 of *Predestination*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 29:1; Deuteronomy 10:8; Deuteronomy 32:8; 1 Chronicles 15:16-19; 1 Chronicles 23:13; Luke 2:40; John 1:14; Acts 13:2; Romans 1:1; Romans 1:11 and 8 more.

items.question: What should someone who just gave their life to Christ learn first?
items.text:
What a joy to hear of a new life in Christ. The books say that anyone who comes to Christ will have to be taught the elementary principles of the faith, and that the way you are taught these fundamentals permanently determines your spiritual make-up [2]. That person is also your first teacher, the one who taught you the fundamentals of Christianity, and is not to be forgotten [2].

It also helps to understand what has actually happened to you: if you are born again, you have had a spiritual heart transplant, and you need understanding of the concept of salvation so that you grow in grace [7]. Wisdom is the principal thing, and you gain understanding when you know principles [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Those Who Forget* and chapter 1 of *Seven Great Principles*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 21:34-36; 1 Corinthians 4:15; Hebrews 5:12.

items.question: Why is it dangerous to think you're untouchable or indispensable in ministry?
items.text:
Thinking you are untouchable is the mindset of a dangerous person: "My father cannot sack me, my father cannot discipline me, my father cannot deal with me" [1]. Absalom felt he could not be sacked or transferred away, and told Joab that if the king found any iniquity in him, "let him kill me" (2 Samuel 14:32) [3]. As soon as you begin to think of yourself as indispensable, you are becoming proud and deceived, and pride always comes before a fall [1].

The danger is real, because God is not bound to keep using you as you are. Do not think that you are indispensable; if you do not do what God wants you to do, your ministry will be taken away from you and given to another — "Take from him the pound, and give it to him that hath ten pounds" (Luke 19:24) [2]. And a true Absalom is not corrected by punishment or years of hard discipline; two years of exile did not change his heart, he became hardened and even more dangerous [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Those who are Dangerous Sons* and chapter 6 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 14:32; Luke 19:24; Romans 11:29.

items.question: What happens when you pray for wisdom?
items.book: Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry
items.text:
When you pray for wisdom, God gives it generously to those who ask, as James 1:5 says [6]. Solomon is the great example: he asked for an understanding heart to judge God's people, and it pleased the Lord that he asked for this rather than long life or riches [6].

The books describe several effects of that prayer. It gives you a large heart, a great depth of understanding and insight [5]. It makes your wisdom excel the wisdom prevailing in your nation, as Solomon's excelled the wisdom of the East and of Egypt [1][5]. It makes you wiser than your contemporaries, as 1 Kings 4:31 says he was wiser than all men [1]. It leads to supernatural abilities and insight, so that you speak proverbs and write songs [1]. It makes you appreciate nature, speaking of trees, beasts, fowl, creeping things and fishes [2]. And it causes people, even kings, to travel from afar to hear the wisdom God has given you [3].

Prayer for wisdom also changes the course of a person's life, delivering them from the curses that govern the masses; when you get wisdom, riches, honour and length of days arrive, as Proverbs 3:13-16 says [4][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 26 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry* and chapter 3 of *How to Pray*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 3:9-11; 1 Kings 4:29-34; Proverbs 3:13-16; Proverbs 8:15; Luke 11:13; 2 Corinthians 4:4; James 1:5.

items.question: How can I avoid becoming too familiar with my leaders or with people I look up to?
items.book: Those Who Pretend, Intimidate And Are Familiar
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and the heart of it is guarding your respect and awe for those you look up to. Familiarity means knowing someone so well that you lose your admiration, respect, and sense of awe, becoming presumptuous [6]. One way to avoid it is to keep a degree of distance: people who frequently interact with a leader, who know too much about him, who are his friends, or who have been promoted are all prone to familiarity [4][5]. Jesus Himself modeled this by making clear distinctions between ranks—He sat on the donkey while the disciples walked, and slept in the boat while they rowed—and these differences are necessary to kill the spirit of familiarity [1][7].

Watch for the subtle signs, and be quick to detect them. Familiarity shows up when a follower tries to direct or correct his leader, as Peter did when he rebuked Jesus [3][5]. When that happened, Jesus brought him down to size urgently, even calling him "Satan" (Matthew 16:23) [3][8]. So address and confront familiarity wherever you find it, and put subordinates who are out of order back into their proper places [8]. Also beware of monotony—repetitiveness and dullness are the perfect contexts for familiarity, so introduce new ideas and break monotonous patterns [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 8 and 10 of *Those Who Pretend, Intimidate And Are Familiar*, chapter 95 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 13 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 41:9; Matthew 16:15-17; Matthew 16:22-23; Mark 1:37-39; Mark 6:1-6.

items.question: What does the anointing do for someone's ministry?
items.text:
The anointing brings supernatural help for your life and ministry, as David said, "I have given help to one who is mighty" (Psalm 89:19b) [1]. It raises you up to heights in ministry and establishes you — "I have found David My servant; With My holy oil I have anointed him. With whom My hand will be established" (Psalm 89:20-21) [1]. It also introduces strength to your ministry, so that "My arm also will strengthen him" (Psalm 89:21) [1], and it protects you from deception, the blindness and hypocrisy Jesus rebuked when He said, "You blind guides, who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel!" (Matthew 23:24) [1].

Beyond that, the anointing enables you to build and restore, laying brick upon brick and making something out of shattered lives [2]. It causes people who are bound to be set free, for logical teaching cannot open prison doors [4], and it comforts those who mourn, so that people are encouraged just by seeing you or hearing you [4]. It restores beauty and attractiveness, so that many are drawn to an anointed pastor's church without knowing why [4]. It reaches beyond your own country and tribe — "strangers shall stand and feed your flocks" (Isaiah 61:5) [2] — and it affects your children, for "I will establish his descendants forever" (Psalm 89:29) [6]. It gives a long-lasting ministry, since "his seed shall endure forever, and his throne as the sun before me" (Psalm 89:36-37) [6]. And it is specific, like a gun: the healing anointing differs from the teaching anointing, which differs from the pastoral anointing [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 15 of *Steps to the Anointing* and chapter 5 of *Catch The Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 89:19-21; Psalms 89:29; Psalms 89:36-37; Isaiah 61:2-3; Isaiah 61:5-6; Matthew 23:24.

items.question: What does the Bible say about the importance of skill for getting things built?
items.text:
Yes, friend, the books speak to this plainly. Skill is the master key to building, and failure to build reveals a lack of practical skills — impractical men build nothing [1][2]. Solomon himself acknowledged he had no one who could skill to hew timber like the Sidonians, and he hired skilled workers for the house of the Lord (2 Chronicles 2:7-8) [1]. Skill is also what determines who is chosen and whether you become ten times better, as with Daniel and his friends, to whom God gave knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom (Daniel 1:17-20) [2].

But building is not by skill alone. The books also say the Church will be built by the power of the Holy Spirit, not by might nor by power (Zechariah 4:6) — not by education, background, location, or strategies [6]. And unless the Lord builds the house, they labour in vain that build it (Psalm 127:1) [4]. So skill matters greatly, yet the labour must rest on God's power.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 15 of *The Determinants*, chapter 64 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 3 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Chronicles 28:10; 1 Chronicles 28:20; 2 Chronicles 2:7-8; Psalms 127:1; Ecclesiastes 9:11; Daniel 1:17-20; Zechariah 4:6; Luke 7:4-5.

items.question: How should a Christian live simply and avoid wasting money?
items.text:
The books speak to this plainly. A steward will one day be asked to give an account of what was in his control, and if he cannot account for it he loses his position [1]. Wasters tend to become poor, while those who halt the wastage tend to become rich [1]. So cut out waste — most poor nations waste half their resources, and that is why they remain poor [6]. Do not have an expensive lifestyle; cut your coat according to your size, and avoid grandiose things others may be doing [6]. Develop a dislike for loans and gifts, for every admirer of gifts and loans is likely to fail in leadership [6]. Learn to do things yourself with your own hands rather than sitting aloof like an executive [6].

Watch your company too, for the prodigal wasted his substance with harlots, and bad company will cause you to waste your life away [3]; as 1 Corinthians 15:33 says, evil company corrupts good habits [3]. And beware the love of money and earthly things, for it is Satan's voice that urges you to spend your life, time, energy and money on everything but God's work [2]. Lust for anything apart from God's Word is dangerous and destroys [5], and there are no short cuts — the Kingdom is like a mustard seed that needs time to die and grow [4].

items.question: How did Paul become equal to or greater than Peter as an apostle?
items.text:
The books say Paul rose to the level of Peter, the chiefest apostle, because the grace of revelation visited Paul rather than Peter, and because Paul laboured more abundantly than all the apostles, as he says in 1 Corinthians 15:10 [1][2]. Peter had disowned Jesus at the crucifixion; though Jesus forgave him, there was a sense in which the power of Jesus lifted from Peter's ministry afterward, and this led to Paul's pre-eminence in the church [1][2].

Another passage describes Paul as a replacement for the missing Judas Iscariot, one "born out of due time," who saw himself as the least of the apostles yet not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles (1 Corinthians 15:8-9; 2 Corinthians 11:5) [3]. Still another says Paul caught up with those ahead of him by the key of wisdom — the wisdom of walking in the grace of God and of working harder than those ahead of him — and that Peter himself acknowledged Paul had been given special wisdom (2 Peter 3:14-16) [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *BEMA Judgment And Justice*, chapter 13 of *JUDAS
Who is he??* and chapter 13 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 34:7; Numbers 5:20-22; 1 Corinthians 15:8-10; 2 Corinthians 11:5; 2 Corinthians 12:11-12; 2 Peter 3:14-16.

items.question: What does it mean to make a C-turn toward Jesus instead of a U-turn away from him?
items.book: What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent
items.text:
A C-turn is a swerve to the side — not a reversal, but a manoeuvre that takes you off the wrong course onto a better way [2][3]. Andrew and John show this: they were disciples of John the Baptist, and when John pointed out the Lamb of God, they did not turn away from the ministry but followed Jesus, and that C-turn took them deeper and further into God (John 1:35-37) [1]. Peter is another example — the fisherman became an apostle because he was willing to swerve off the layman's road and into full-time ministry, leaving his nets immediately when Jesus said, "Follow Me, and I will make you fishers of men" (Matthew 4:18-20) [3].

A U-turn, by contrast, is a reversal of your former decisions — the prodigal son reversing his course and humbly returning to his proper place (Luke 15:18-20), or Zacchaeus turning away from corruption and swindling (Luke 19:8) [4]. That kind of turn is true repentance, and if you cannot make U-turns you cannot repent from your mistakes [4]. So a C-turn is not turning away from Jesus; it is being flexible enough to shift off a wrong course onto a better one as you follow Him [2][3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 4:18-20; Luke 8:37; Luke 15:18-20; Luke 19:8; John 1:35-37.

items.question: What does it mean to be a person of faith?
items.text:
Being a person of faith is closely tied to obedience: faith is equated with obedience, and an obedient person is a man of faith — obeying God is the exercising of your faith [1]. When you do not believe, you are disobedient [1].

It also shows up in your attitude, since your attitude is a clear revelation of your faith and beliefs, and to have faith in God means to have a good attitude [2]. And it takes great faith to carry on in prayer, for anyone who persists in prayer is a man of faith [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1 and 10 of *Faith Secrets* and chapter 5 of *Pr 6. Prayer Opportunities*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 9:22-23; Hebrews 11:1.

items.question: How do I become anointed by the Holy Spirit?
items.text:
Friend, our books point to several things, and I'll give them to you just as they are.

Being led by the Holy Spirit is central: "To arrive at the place of the anointing, you will need to be led by the Holy Spirit," and this is the distinguishing feature of anointed men [4]. That leading may take you where you would not naturally choose, for Jesus was led by the Spirit into a wilderness, and you must become someone who can follow the Spirit even against your natural inclinations [1]. Waiting on God is another step, for the disciples had to wait in Jerusalem, and Isaiah 40:31 promises that those who wait on the Lord gain new strength [2]. Unity matters too, since the Spirit fell at Pentecost when they were all with one accord in one place (Acts 2:1) [2]. And hearing with faith: "You receive the Spirit by the hearing of faith," as one man soaked in messages on the anointing until he was saturated [3].

Yet our books also say plainly that God decides: "No matter how hard you work or follow certain principles, God divinely chooses whom He will allow to come close to Him," for He is a God who hides Himself (Isaiah 45:15), and you must ask, seek, and knock [8]. So keep following, keep waiting, keep listening — and look to Him who chooses.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 5 and 8 of *Steps to the Anointing* and chapter 13 of *Seeing And Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 28:1; Isaiah 40:31; Isaiah 45:15; Matthew 4:1; Luke 4:1-15; Acts 1:4; Acts 2:1.

items.question: Different topic: how do I pray effectively?
items.text:
Yes, let's turn to prayer. The books say not all prayers are effective — some are just doodling and dawdling, and you might as well say "twinkle, twinkle little star" if your prayers are not going to work [1]. So here is what they give us.

Pray strategic Bible prayers, letting your prayers be guided by the Word of God — for instance the prayers in Ephesians 1:17-19 and Ephesians 3:15-19, the latter grounding you in love, since even giving your body to be burned profits nothing without charity (1 Corinthians 13:3) [1]. Pray fervently — ardently, with passion and feeling, so that anyone watching could describe your prayer as burning or eager [2]. Pray in tongues, as Paul boasted, "I thank God that I speak in tongues more than you all" (1 Corinthians 14:18) [2]. And have discussions with the Holy Spirit, for prayer is a two-way affair; the Comforter will teach you all things and bring all things to your remembrance (John 14:26) [2].

The books also speak of praying without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17) — on the bus, in the office, in the shower — and of Daniel's pattern: prayer must be habitual to be effective, and everyone must develop the ability and formulae for praying four times a day, morning, afternoon, evening and all-the-time [3][5]. Jesus rose a great while before day and went to a solitary place to pray (Mark 1:35), and He continued all night in prayer to God (Luke 6:12) [5][8]. There are also short, powerful prayers for crisis moments, as when Jesus thanked the Father at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:41,42) and then acted boldly [8]. And when it comes to the will of God, pray repeatedly and for hours — Jesus prayed the same words three times, and these were not vain repetitions (Matthew 6:7) but valuable, effective repetition [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Transform Your Pastoral Ministry*, chapters 1 and 7 of *How to Pray* and chapter 2 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 6:7; Mark 1:35; Luke 6:12-13; John 11:41-42; 1 Corinthians 13:3; 1 Corinthians 14:18; Ephesians 1:17-19; Ephesians 3:15-19; 1 Thessalonians 5:17; James 5:16.

items.question: How do I know God will take me back after I've turned away from him?
items.text:
Our books speak to this. God promises mercy to those who love Him, and to receive mercy is to have your sins forgotten and ignored as though they never happened; through the blood of Jesus your sins will be washed away [8]. He is the faithful God who keeps covenant and mercy with them that love Him, as Deuteronomy 7:9-10 says [8].

There is also a picture of God restoring what was lost: He knows your irreplaceable loss, and He has not forgotten you — He will replace the irreplaceable [1]. And He is a God who rights every wrong, keeping a record of all that has happened, and He will right all the wrongs [2].

If you have turned away, the passages hold out both His mercy toward those who love Him [8] and His promise to restore [1][2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 11 and 15 of *TS2. Hope Secrets* and chapter 12 of *If You Love The Lord*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 7:9-10; Isaiah 49:20-21; Hebrews 10:30-36.

items.question: How can I grow spiritually and bear fruit as a Christian?
items.text:
What a good thing to long for. Our books say plainly that every Christian should aim to be fruitful, because Christ saved us so that we would go and bear fruit, and that our fruit should remain (John 15:16) [5]. So let me share what they say about how that growth happens.

You grow by abiding. Jesus said the branch cannot bear fruit of itself except it abide in the vine, and that he who abides brings forth much fruit (John 15:4, 5) — to abide means to stay, to be planted, to remain in Christ and continue in the things of God [4]. A tree has to be nurtured in one place over time before it can bear fruit; no mango tree bears after just one year [4]. So be stable in church, be permanent, and make a quality decision to be planted in a Spirit-filled, Bible-believing church, remaining rooted until your fruits begin to show [3]. Those planted in the house of the LORD shall still bring forth fruit in old age (Psalm 92:13, 14) [3].

You also grow by maturing. A Christian without converts is immature, and an immature Christian runs from church to church and programme to programme looking for excitement, blown about by every wind of doctrine [1]. It is time to grow up and put away childish things, as 1 Corinthians 13:11 says [4]. Set spiritual goals and press toward the mark of the high calling (Philippians 3:13, 14), for Christians with no spiritual ambition tend to become fruitless [5]. And get active — passive Christians bear no fruits; witnessing, teaching, and helping in the church will all help you get active in the things of God [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *Many Are Called* and chapter 9 of *How you can become a strong Christian*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 92:13-14; John 15:4-5; John 15:16; 1 Corinthians 13:11; Philippians 3:13-14; Colossians 1:10.

items.question: How can a young person deal with sexual desires and stay pure?
items.text:
What a good and honest question. The books speak to this directly, and they speak with respect for what you are feeling, not shame.

First, they tell you to respect your sexuality rather than deny it. Desires are powerful forces, and a proper respect for youthful lusts, rather than a denial of them, will save you from them [4]. Lust is an animal desire for sexual indulgence, and if you do not respect these instincts they will overwhelm you and lead you away from God's plan for your life [2]. Scripture is plain here: "Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart" (2 Timothy 2:22) [2][5].

Second, they call you to actively flee and to set your will on purity. The will of God is your sanctification, "that you abstain from sexual immorality" (1 Thessalonians 4:3-4), and since that is one of the clearest directions of the Lord, you should make it one of your clearest and most energetic goals to practically live a sexually pure life [6]. Stay away from anyone who would want such a relationship with you, and find out what God's will is for your own journey of staying away from fornication — it may be never reading certain books or watching certain films, it may be marrying young, it may be avoiding certain friends or certain work situations [6]. And do not trifle with this subject: Paul was emphatic that immorality brings the wrath of God (Ephesians 5:5-6) [4].

Third, and this is your hope: holiness does not come from age. Holiness is engineered by the Spirit of holiness, not by being an older person, and age has nothing to do with holiness [7]. Young people can be empowered by the Spirit of holiness and can live free from sin — God says, "I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes" (Ezekiel 36:27) [7]. Joseph was only eighteen when Potiphar's wife tried to have sex with him, and he is held up as an example in purity [1]. This is your chance to demonstrate that you can live free of fornication and immorality [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 10, 12, 13 and 20 of *Ready@20* and chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing*.

items.question: Why should we not boast about our own strength or willpower when we survive something?
items.text:
Our books speak to this plainly. When people credited a man's survival to his resilience and strong willpower, he died of a heart attack a week later, and the question was asked, "Where was his strong will power?" [1]. God does not like it when you boast about things He has given you as though you did not receive them, as 1 Corinthians 4:7 says: "What hast thou that thou didst not receive? If thou didst receive it then why dost thou boast as though thou didst not receive it?" [1].

When a Christian continues to boast about his strength, Satan hears him and decides to test him; where you are over-confident is where you can be the weakest, because you have dropped your guard [2][3]. Staying on the right track is largely by the grace of God, and not by your own strength, so "let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:12) [2][3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 12 of *Those who are Proud*, chapter 3 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 5 of *Backsliding*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 1:20; 1 Corinthians 4:7; 1 Corinthians 10:12.

items.question: How should a pastor plan church finances when people don't pay the money they pledged?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak plainly to this. A wise pastor should never budget on what the congregation has pledged, because most members will not pay what they promised, and you should expect no more than 30% of pledges to come in [1][2][6]. Pastors who budget on promised amounts are usually accused of misusing funds because the full amounts are never realized [1][2].

Instead, the build-up of your regular tithes and offerings should be the main source of project financing, and fund-raising should be seen as a boost to your existing financial situation, since God has determined that the church is to be financed through regular tithes and offerings [1][2][6]. It is also wise to save money towards a project before embarking on fund-raising for it, so that your project comes on whether the people pay up their pledges or not [1][2]. And when you do take pledges, the shorter the time given to honour them, the higher the returns tend to be; a period of one week to three months is recommended [2][6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 12 of *Church Growth* and chapter 6 of *Church Administration*.

items.question: How can we grow our church like the early church did?
items.text:
What a good desire, pastor. The early church gives us the pattern: after the apostles prayed and laid hands on the seven, "the word of God increased; and the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem greatly" (Acts 6:6-7), and "the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved" (Acts 2:47) [1][3]. So growth came as the word was preached and God added to them.

A few things our books press on: church growth is a priority because Jesus said, "I will build my church and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it" [1]. It is hard and must be fought for, not expected by osmosis — your church will grow through a series of systematic, aggressive campaigns with a specific purpose [2][4]. It helps to create a Church Growth Office that monitors things like attendance, income, branches, small groups, and active members, so you can ensure the church increases rather than decreases [3]. And don't despise small beginnings: the kingdom is like a mustard seed, the least of seeds that becomes a great tree (Matthew 13:31-32), and one pastor whose megachurch began with a single attendee is a picture of that [5][7]. Don't be in a hurry — no tree grows into a large tree overnight [5][7].

One practical starting point: take your "tangerine segments" — the naturally formed groups like the choir, ushers, or those living near the church — and grow those, since if your choir is very large, your church will be very large [6]. And as you grow, accept that many will be once-a-week "Group B" members; love them anyway, preach sermons they can appreciate, and pray for them [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 62 and 64 of *The Gift Of Governments*, chapter 11 of *Attempt Great Things for God*, chapters 4 and 26 of *The Double Mega Missionary Church*, chapters 7 and 13 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 20 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Jeremiah 30:19; Matthew 13:31-32; Acts 2:41; Acts 2:47; Acts 4:4; Acts 6:6-7; Acts 13:44; Acts 16:5.

items.question: Why do some pastors keep moving from place to place or stay far from home?
items.book: Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order
items.text:
Some pastors move from place to place because a transfer is meant to set things in order and improve the life of the pastor and the church, as Titus 1:5 says, "that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting" [7]. A bishop may also transfer a pastor who cannot break through and flourish in a town, since a move may break a cycle of barrenness, or transfer one who cannot live in purity there, to break cycles of immorality [7]. Others move because they are searching for their Rehoboth, the place God has designed for them where they will become fruitful, as Genesis 26:22 says, "for now the Lord hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land" [1].

But the books also describe other reasons. Some move to be where their history or background is not known [3]. Some are on the run from a troubled marriage, moving again and again in an attempt to control a Jezebel in the home, or living a seven-hour flight away from a wife, or leaving the church and country like Elijah on the run [8]. And some who struggle with being transferred are agitated by spirits of rebellion, like Absalom, who said, "it had been good for me to have been there still" [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 10 of *Opportunities*, chapter 16 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry*, chapter 59 of *The Gift Of Governments* and chapter 18 of *The Beauty The Beast and The Pastor*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 26:22; Genesis 28:16; 2 Samuel 14:31-32; 1 Kings 21:18-19; 1 Chronicles 12:33; Matthew 16:26; Titus 1:5.

items.question: How old were Jesus' disciples when he called them?
items.text:
The books give us some clues here. From the Mishnah's stages of a young man's life, most of the disciples may have been below eighteen, with some as young as fifteen, since Peter is the only one known to have been married and no other disciple seemed to have had a wife or mother-in-law [1][3]. Peter himself likely started his ministry at about the age of twenty, since Jesus paid the temple tax for Himself and Peter only, and the tax applied to those twenty and up (Exodus 30:12-14) [5].

The books also say the disciples were probably younger than Jesus, and that Peter, James, John and the others became apostles when they were young men [2]. They note there is no evidence in Scripture for a specific age for any of the disciples, so these are clues rather than certainties [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *The Word Of My Patience* and chapter 6 of *Seven Great Principles*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 30:12-14; Matthew 8:14-15; Matthew 17:24-27; Luke 5:10; Luke 7:28; 1 Corinthians 4:1; Revelation 3:10.

items.question: How can I deal with people in my church who criticize the pastor behind his back?
items.text:
Our books speak to this plainly. Scripture says, "speak evil of no man" (Titus 3:2), and we are warned not to criticize or ridicule those we invite, nor to entertain negative comments about ministers while they are with us or after they are gone [1]. The book of Proverbs tells us, "For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he" (Proverbs 23:7), and such negatively-minded people who constantly discuss the pastor behind his back will not pay tithes [2].

There is also a stronger word: "Show me a church filled with critical people and I will show you a church filled with demons" [7]. And where a person is scornful, mocking and not believing in you, the biblical remedy is not prayer or fasting but to act on Proverbs 22:10 — "CAST OUT THE SCORNER, and contention shall go out" [4]. Yet another passage counsels patience, noting that criticism often comes from immaturity or inexperience, and that Jesus did not rebuke His disciples for abandoning Him but gave them another chance, sending them into the "school of hard knocks" [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 22 of *Church Growth*, chapter 4 of *Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich*, chapters 4 and 7 of *Those Who Are Ignorant* and chapter 10 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 1:1; Proverbs 22:10; Proverbs 23:7; Proverbs 26:15; Mark 14:27-31; Romans 13:1; Titus 3:2.

items.question: What does the Bible say about people who were born and raised in the church?
items.text:
What a blessing it is to be born in the house of God. The eighty-seventh psalm speaks of the spiritual blessings that follow young people who were born in the house, and it says "This and that man was born in her: and the highest himself shall establish her" [2]. So those born in the house are going to be greatly established, and glorious things are spoken of them, as Psalm 87:3 says [1]. The Lord shall count them among the great when He writes up the people, as Psalm 87:6 says [1]. They will also produce good music — singers and players on instruments shall be there, as Psalm 87:7 says [1].

Being born in a particular church and growing up in it to become a leader in the same church is a prophetic blessing God is giving you [2]. A young man born in the house will have his foundation in the holy mountain of God, and though Satan may threaten to destroy him with sex, he will stand sure because he has a solid foundation in holiness [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Ready@20*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 87:1-7.

items.question: How can I show appreciation to the people in my life before it's too late?
items.text:
What a good question to ask while there is still time. The books urge you to value people before you lose them, and to look into your life to see whether there is anybody you need to value — then locate them and find a suitable way of expressing appreciation, hopefully before it is too late to make amends [1][2]. Mary honoured Jesus in time, and the counsel is plain: if you want to honour someone, rush to do so now [3].

The example held up is a son who could say he had said all he could have said to his father, and had the best of relationships with him [1][2]. And the deepest way to say thank you is not with words alone — the only way you can say "Thank you" is with your life, giving something genuine that comes from you [5]. So let your gratitude be reasonable, a reasonable service offered to God [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 4 of *Frugality*, chapter 13 of *Those Who Honour You* and chapter 4 of *How Can I Say Thanks*.

items.question: How do I experience God's presence when I don't feel Him near?
items.text:
I hear the ache in that question, and I want to walk with you through what our books actually say.

The presence of God is real and can be felt — He is Jehovah Shammah, "The Lord is there," and it is possible to grow in your ability to experience Him, in your room, in your meetings, at home [2][4]. His presence is like dew: invisible, yet you can see its effects in your life [2]. So even when you don't sense Him, His presence may still be at work.

Our books also point to things that draw His presence near. Where salvation and redemption are preached and believed, the presence of God is felt — you can practically invoke His presence by believing in the atoning blood of Jesus [5][8]. Being under a covering, relating humbly to the pastor or father God places over you, is another way His presence is experienced; a man with no covering will not experience the presence of God in his ministry [3]. And sins of the flesh and pride cause many to lose His presence [6].

If you'd like, tell me more about your situation, and we can look together at what the books say about it.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 13 of *The Anointing and the Presence* and chapters 11 and 14 of *Steps to God's Presence*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 33:14-15; Ezekiel 48:35; Hosea 14:5-6; Zechariah 11:12; Matthew 27:8-9; Luke 5:17; 1 Corinthians 1:27-29.

items.question: How can I keep from becoming bitter and turning away from God when I go through hard times?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this very thing, and the heart of it is this: suffering is a test, and it brings out what is in you [5]. When you receive what they call the contradiction of sinners — something contrary to what you expected after doing good — be careful, and do not turn against God [1]. Jesus Himself endured the contradiction of sinners and showed us how to endure it, as Hebrews 12:3 says [1].

Do not become bitter, and do not let bitterness move you away from God, for Hebrews 12:15 warns lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled [3]. When you walk in forgiveness you attract God's mercy, but when bitterness is in your spirit you will no longer receive from God and He no longer answers your prayers [2]. So maintain a sweet spirit and learn to live without bitterness [2]. Remember too that God led Israel to the bitter waters of Marah on purpose, and it was there that many fell away; do not fall away because of the bitterness you experience, for God loves you and knows why He brings you to that place [4]. And do not murmur or complain, for murmuring reveals a bad attitude and turns into bitterness [6]. Instead, put on the new man, in whom there is forgiveness and love instead of bitterness [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Losing, Suffering, Sacrificing and Dying*, chapter 10 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*, chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapters 26 and 30 of *Why Few Are Chosen* and chapter 2 of *Tasters And Partakers*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 8:2; Hebrews 12:3; Hebrews 12:15.

items.question: How can I pray more effectively?
items.text:
Prayer that works is not doodling and dawdling — it is effectual, fervent prayer, and James 5:16 says the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much [1]. So let your prayers be guided by the Word of God, praying the very prayers recorded in Scripture, like the ones in Ephesians 1:17-19 and Ephesians 3:15-19 [1]. Pray fervently — ardently, with passion and feeling, so that anyone watching could describe your prayer as burning and eager [3]. And spend time praying in tongues, as Paul boasted, "I thank God that I speak in tongues more than you all" (1 Corinthians 14:18) [3].

Prayer is also meant to be a two-way affair: learn to speak to the Holy Spirit and to hear His voice, for as Jesus said, the Comforter "shall teach you all things" (John 14:26) [3]. Make it habitual — pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17), on the bus, in the office, in the shower [4]. And develop the ability to pray four times a day: morning, afternoon, evening, and all-the-time [6]. Jesus Himself rose a great while before day and went to a solitary place to pray (Mark 1:35) [6][8], and He continued all night in prayer to God (Luke 6:12,13) [6]. Watching and praying — staying awake at night to pray — will make you a mighty prayer warrior [8].

items.question: If I do good things for others, how will I be rewarded?
items.book: He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this in a few ways, and they don't all say the same thing, so let me lay them out for you.

One answer is that you should not look to people for your reward at all. "Do not look to people for gratitude. A leader looks to God for rewards," and Scripture says your rewards depend on God, not on the people you helped — "Knowing that whatsoever good thing any man doeth, the same shall he receive of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:8) [2]. The same counsel appears again: "Do not expect gratitude from man; expect your rewards from God" [7].

Another answer is that the reward for faithfulness is often more work, not rest. God sees your faithfulness with what belongs to others and rewards you with more labor in your own ministry — "if ye have not been faithful in that which is another man's, who shall give you that which is your own?" (Luke 16:12) [5].

And a third thread warns that doing good does not guarantee a warm return in this life. Jesus did many good works and was rewarded with hatred and wickedness [1][6], and Jeremiah was repaid with a pit [1][4]. Yet there is a curse for those who repay good with evil: "Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein" (Proverbs 26:27) [4][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *How Can I Say Thanks*, chapter 101 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 5 of *WOM15. The Reward for Hard Work is More Work* and chapter 5 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*.

items.question: Why do the people closest to a pastor, like family and his wife, often have a hard time receiving from his ministry?
items.text:
This is a painful thing to watch, and our books speak to it plainly. Familiarity is the root of it: people who know you closely often cannot receive from you, saying in their hearts, "Is this not Dag? We know him and we know his class" [6]. Relatives say, "Is this not Azoyzoy's son? We carried him when he was a baby," and with that background, how can such people receive him as a man of God [8]?

Pastors' wives often suffer from severe familiarity too — like Michal, they are not impressed with their husbands when everyone else is impressed, saying, "I know you. No one knows you better than I do" [8]. In a sense they are right about all these things, but the fact is that they have become victims of familiarity [8]. Even Jesus could do no mighty work in His hometown; they knew Him too well to receive Him as the Son of God, and were offended at Him (Mark 6:1-3, 5) [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *Church Planting* and chapter 13 of *Ministerial Barrenness*.

items.question: I keep saying hurtful things when I am angry. How do I control my mouth?
items.text:
What you're describing is real, and Scripture takes the tongue seriously: it is "an unruly evil, full of deadly poison" (James 3:8), and no man can tame it on his own — it takes the Holy Spirit to help the believer control his tongue [3]. So the first honest step is to stop trusting your own strength for this.

The books also tie angry words to something deeper. Wrath and anger are signs of lingering unforgiveness, and we are told to put away all bitterness, wrath, anger, clamour and evil speaking, being kind and tenderhearted, forgiving one another even as God for Christ's sake has forgiven us (Ephesians 4:31-32) [5]. And "let not the sun go down upon your wrath" (Ephesians 4:26) — living in silence or letting offence sit only deepens the strain; the call is to walk in forgiveness [1]. Practically, the books urge you to be aware of the potential for evil in your flesh, to fast regularly, and to give no opportunity to the flesh, since "neither give place to the devil" (Ephesians 4:27) [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 60 of *Model Marriage*, chapter 1 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue*, chapter 4 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition* and chapter 2 of *Seven Great Principles*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Corinthians 10:5; Galatians 5:13; Ephesians 4:26-27; Ephesians 4:29; Ephesians 4:31-32; James 3:8.

Wrath and anger are signs of lingering unforgiveness, and we are told to put away all bitterness, wrath, anger, clamour and evil speaking, being kind and tenderhearted, forgiving one another even as God for Christ's sake has forgiven us (Ephesians 4:31-32).
And "let not the sun go down upon your wrath" (Ephesians 4:26) — living in silence or letting offence sit only deepens the strain; the call is to walk in forgiveness.

Practically, the books urge you to be aware of the potential for evil in your flesh, to fast regularly, and to give no opportunity to the flesh, since "neither give place to the devil" (Ephesians 4:27).

items.question: How can I stay close to God and keep bearing fruit in my life?
items.text:
What a good question to be asking, pastor. Our books speak to this directly, and they keep pointing to one thing: staying close.

The Lord Jesus said, "He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit" (John 15:5), and abiding simply means staying in God — not being in and out of Him, but staying committed [1]. Closeness is a law of fruit bearing: as the branch cannot bear fruit of itself except it abide in the vine, so it is with us (John 15:4-5) [3]. The closer you get to God, the closer you are to the anointing, and the closer you will be to bearing fruit [1][3]. Draw nigh to God and He will draw nigh to you (James 4:8) — so take time to wait on the Lord [1].

Staying connected to Jesus is the master key; human effort can never substitute for it, and disconnection and detachment are the master keys to withering [2][4]. The longer you abide, the more fruitful you become — experienced pastors who have abided in Christ much longer can generate a larger church much faster than a young, inexperienced one [1]. And remember that God has linked answered prayer to fruit bearing: He chose and ordained us to go and bring forth fruit that should remain, "that whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you" (John 15:16) [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Fruitfulness (2022)*, chapter 6 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make*, chapter 14 of *Victory Secrets* and chapter 3 of *100% Answered Prayer*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 127:1; Mark 12:34; John 15:4-6; John 15:16; James 4:8; James 5:16; Revelation 1:20.

items.question: How can I be sure I really know the Lord and won't be turned away from heaven?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this very thing. The assurance they hold out is not in how much you do for God, but in whether you truly know Him and are known by Him. Jesus uses His personal knowledge of you as a basis for judgment, and "being known is one of the highest qualifications for serving God" [1]. Many will say "Lord, Lord," having prophesied and done wonderful works in His name, yet He will profess, "I never knew you" (Matthew 7:22-23) [2][3]. So it is possible to be a member and do great things but not know God [3][4].

The way the books point to is a personal relationship, pursued daily. "A daily quiet time will make you have a personal relationship with the Lord. Nothing else can make you have a personal relationship with the Lord" [3][4]. Coming to church a thousand times is different from a personal, one-to-one interaction with Him [3][4]. A quiet time will save you from the delusion that working for God is the same as knowing Him, and will prevent you from going to hell [3][4]. It is up to you to draw near to Him on a daily basis, for as James 4:8 says, "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you" [4]. And through the blood of Jesus you are cleansed from your sins so that you can know God [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Weeping and Gnashing*, chapter 30 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*, chapter 4 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day* and chapter 5 of *The Secret*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 7:21-23; Luke 13:25-28; 2 Timothy 1:8-9; James 4:8; Revelation 3:20.

items.question: What does the wind of the Holy Spirit do in a person's life?
items.text:
The wind of the Spirit does many things in a person's life. It blows away death, as when God made a wind to pass over the earth and the waters assuaged (Genesis 8:1-3) [1]. It makes a way for you when you seem trapped, as the Lord caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind (Exodus 14:21) [1]. It causes anything that displeases God to wither, like the seven ears blasted with the east wind (Genesis 41:22-23) [2], and it drives away demonic powers, as the Lord turned a mighty strong west wind which took away the locusts (Exodus 10:16-19) [2]. It dries up the evil springs of the enemy, for the wind of the Lord shall come up from the wilderness and his spring shall become dry (Hosea 13:15) [3], and it destroys the enemy's forces, for the Lord will raise up a destroying wind against Babylon and shall empty her land (Jeremiah 51:1-2) [5]. It also brings in the supplies you need, as through the wind of the Spirit Moses was able to feed two million people [5].

When the wind of the Holy Spirit blows on you, you start to see, you start to hear and you start to feel [7]. There will be activity, for a sign of the presence of the breath of the Spirit is lots of activity (Genesis 7:21-22) [7], and there will be growth, for wherever there is life there is growth (Psalms 104:29) [7]. The wind of the Spirit is mysterious, powerful in movement, independent, invisible, varied in direction, makes a sound that tells you where He is going, and brings on the fire of God (John 3:8; Acts 2:2-4) [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 6 of *Flow in the Anointing*.

items.question: What can I learn from Esther about helping others even when I'm comfortable?
items.text:
Friend, the books hold Esther up as a picture of someone God raised into comfort and privilege for a purpose beyond herself. Mordecai's warning to her was plain: if you hold your peace at this time, deliverance will arise from another place, but you and your father's house will be destroyed — and who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this [1][5][8]. Her comfort was not the point; she was made queen so she could help "others" [1].

She did hesitate at first, explaining the rules of the palace and the risk of approaching the king uninvited [5]. But she was a novice who listened to her counsellor, and she held on to that counsel [6]. In the end she called for fasting and said, "if I perish, I perish" [2][7]. The books say she is remembered not because she was a queen — there have been many queens — but because she risked her life and her position for the sake of others [1]. And a daughter of destiny does not quickly forget where she came from; she remembers her father and helps him [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Others*, chapter 33 of *Daughter, You Can Make It*, chapter 4 of *Not A Novice* and chapter 14 of *The Art of Following*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 19:32; Esther 4:13-16; Luke 22:24-27.

items.question: Why is it so hard to leave a church that feels like family?
items.text:
It's hard because when a church truly becomes a family, leaving it is like leaving your own flesh and blood. Jesus said His family are those who do the will of His Father — His brothers, sisters, and mothers (Matthew 12:48-50) — and no one leaves a family until they die [1]. That is why faithfulness unto death is a natural occurrence for families, and why people say of such a church, "No one can leave that church" [1].

Every family has its problems — conflicts and misunderstandings — but there is simply no way you can leave your family; you are part of it whether you like it or not, and a misunderstanding with your uncle does not lead you to change your name [2]. So members are taught that hurts and misunderstandings should not make them change their churches, because family members belong together in a lifetime commitment [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Be Thou Faithful Unto Death* and chapter 11 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 5:5; Matthew 12:48-50; 1 Corinthians 3:9; Ephesians 5:31.

items.question: Can God heal emotional wounds and mental problems that medicine can't fix?
items.book: Amplify Your Ministry with Miracles And Manifestations Of The Holy Spirit
items.text:
Yes, friend, the books speak to this clearly and with great hope.

God can heal what man cannot heal. The medicines psychiatrists give often only sedate the patient or improve their mood, and there is no real healing for the psychological and emotional problem, but God can heal what man cannot heal [2]. The psychiatrist is the doctor with fewest answers, yet God reaches to the innermost parts of our being and heals the brokenhearted, and He restores our soul, as Psalm 23:3 says [3]. A daily dose of God's powerful Word will bring healing to every inner wound, for He sent His word and healed them, as Psalm 107:20 says [1].

The books also say God is not against medicine. The two streams of healing are ordained of God and are not contrary to each other, and the intelligence given to human beings to develop drugs is from God [5][8]. So you need not set the two against each other; you need both the power and the wisdom [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day* and chapters 1, 15 and 17 of *Amplify Your Ministry with Miracles And Manifestations Of The Holy Spirit*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Kings 2:19-22; Psalms 23:3; Psalms 107:20; Psalms 147:3; Jeremiah 17:14; Mark 5:2-3; 1 Corinthians 1:24.

items.question: How can I spend time with God every morning without getting bored?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
What a good question, pastor — the books speak to this very thing. The key is not to rely on feeling but on the Word itself: your spirit grows by being fed on the Word of God, so let it enter through a daily Quiet Time of Bible study and prayer, and by listening to preaching, for "faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God" (Romans 10:17) [1]. A daily dose of the Word will increase your faith, and a daily quiet time drives away weariness, dejection and depression — the Word is like rain and snow that cools and refreshes (Isaiah 55:10) [7].

It also helps to see the morning time as a habit rather than a mood: praying at dawn is very repeatable, something you can do tomorrow and every day of the year, even on your busiest days [4]. Daniel knelt and prayed three times a day "as he did aforetime" (Daniel 6:10) [3], and good habits are difficult to form but easy to live with [3]. Jesus Himself rose "a great while before day" and went to a solitary place to pray (Mark 1:35) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *How to be Born again & Avoid Hell*, chapters 1 and 6 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day* and chapter 13 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 3:1-3; Isaiah 55:10; Daniel 6:10; Mark 1:34-36; Romans 1:16; Romans 10:17; 1 Peter 2:2.

items.question: How can I tell if someone is really a Christian or just going to church?
items.text:
That's a question the books speak to plainly. We can distinguish genuine Christians from counterfeit Christians by looking at their fruits, as Matthew 7:20 says, "Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them" [1][2][3][4]. If, by your spiritual activity, others just like you are brought to the Lord and discipled, then this fruit shows that you are real; but if you have no converts to show for your Christianity, then there must be something missing [1][2][3].

The books also warn that church membership does not prove you are a genuine Christian at all, and that real Christianity takes place outside the church after Sundays, with each weekday having its share of prayer, worship, Bible reading and labouring for the Lord [1][5]. They point to 2 Corinthians 13:5: "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith" [1][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *Many Are Called* and chapter 3 of *Bearing Fruit After Your Kind*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 7:20; 2 Corinthians 13:5.

items.question: Why can't I get to heaven by being a good person?
items.text:
Dear friend, the books speak plainly to this. Being a good person and doing good works is not the way to Heaven; good works will not take you there, because "all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags" (Isaiah 64:6) [1][2][7]. We are saved by grace through faith, "not of works, lest any man should boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9) [3][7]. The only way is through the blood of Jesus [1][2][7].

Yet notice this too: the same Scripture that says we are not saved by works says we are "created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them" (Ephesians 2:8-10) [3][4]. So good works do not save us, but after we are saved, God has good works for us to do [3][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 65 and 111 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*, chapter 1 of *Tell Them* and chapters 2 and 3 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 11:16; Proverbs 11:4-5; Isaiah 42:17; Isaiah 64:6; Matthew 7:21-22; Matthew 15:8; Mark 7:6-7; Luke 9:24; Acts 4:12; Romans 3:10 and 3 more.

items.question: What happens if I dishonour my husband?
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this, and it is sobering. Dishonour brings a loss of your place: Vashti did not honour her husband, she lost her position, and she was replaced by a more humble person — the reward for dishonour is to lose your place [1][3]. Dishonour also results in being lightly esteemed, for as 1 Samuel 2:30 says, "them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed" [1].

There is more. Dishonour opens a door to demonic invasion — Jesus said He did not have a devil because He honoured His Father (John 8:49-50), and when Vashti dishonoured her husband, the devils of demotion invaded her life [2]. It also brings obscurity, for Proverbs 20:20 says whoever curses his father or mother, "his lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness" [6]. And a wife who does not adapt herself to her husband is dishonouring him [4]; when your husband is disgraced, you are disgraced as well, for when his face is dragged in the mud, so is yours [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 6 and 11 of *Those Who Honour You* and chapter 31 of *Daughter, You Can Make It*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 32:17; Ruth 3:1-4; 1 Samuel 2:30; Esther 1:15-20; Proverbs 20:20; Luke 22:3; John 8:49-50.

items.question: Why does the Bible warn against trying to get rich?
items.book: Labour to be blessed…labour not to be rich
items.text:
The books give several reasons. Ill-gotten riches can cut your life short — "he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days" (Jeremiah 17:10-11) [1]. Earthly riches can turn you into a fool, as in the parable of the man with full barns to whom God said, "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee" (Luke 12:16-21) [1][2]. Riches can prevent you from taking up your cross and following Jesus; Jesus said, "How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!" (Mark 10:17-23) [5]. And riches are deceptive — "the deceitfulness of riches... choke the word, and it becometh unfruitful" (Mark 4:19) [5].

They are also linked to temptation and a snare: "they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is the root of all evil" (1 Timothy 6:9-10) [3][4]. So the instruction stands: "Labour not to be rich" (Proverbs 23:4) [7]. Instead, labour to be blessed, for "the blessing of the Lord makes rich" (Proverbs 10:22) [6].

items.question: How do I meditate on the Bible and get something out of it during my quiet time?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
What a good thing to want, pastor. The books say plainly that if you do not think about what you are reading, you will lose a major blessing of the Word of God, and Paul told Timothy to think about the Word of God — "Consider what I say; and the Lord give thee understanding in all things" (2 Timothy 2:7) [1][2][3].

Practically, they counsel you to read the passage slowly, not to read a very long passage unless it is necessary, and to stop at any verse that strikes you and think about it — God's Word is so powerful that a single word in a verse is enough to change your life, so each quiet time should be a search for that single word [1][2][3]. Think about the meanings of the words you are reading, and think about how the Scripture applies to life in your generation [1][2][3]. Whisper to the Holy Spirit, asking Him to help you understand the Word and for the Spirit of wisdom and revelation (Ephesians 1:17) [1][2][3]. Then decide on a practical way to implement what you have learned, for without thinking of a way to apply the Scripture directly you will often not benefit from your quiet time [1][2][6]. One of the books also describes staying at the word or phrase that strikes you and turning it over in your mind till the full revelation comes [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapter 8 of *Key Facts for New Believers*, chapter 3 of *The Secret* and chapter 10 of *One Thousand Micro Churches*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 119:18; Ephesians 1:17; 2 Timothy 2:7.

items.question: How can I cooperate with the anointing for dreams and visions?
items.text:
The key is to accept, believe in, and flow with the visions and dreams God gives you, rather than despising them [1]. Daniel wrote his dream down because he respected it, and writing something down shows how seriously you take it [1]. So don't dismiss a dream just because it seems vague or strange — we all have vague and unclear dreams from the Lord, and the drive to obey them is the drive toward the anointing [2].

Obey what you're given: if we obeyed the visions and dreams God gave us, we would experience the anointing, and each one takes you a step closer on the journey [2]. Flow with your dreams and visions, because they are God's instruments encouraging you along the road to the anointing [3]. Be careful, though, to wait on the Lord rather than being moved by dreams you generate out of your own needs and desires — hungry people dream about food and thirsty people dream about drink [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 15 of *The Art of Following*, chapter 6 of *Steps to the Anointing* and chapter 18 of *How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: Job 4:13; Daniel 7:1-4; Acts 10:7-8; Acts 10:13-15; Acts 10:32; Acts 10:48.

items.question: How do I get angels to intervene in my situation when I pray?
items.text:
Friend, our books speak to this plainly: prayer itself is the great and definite way of securing angelic intervention. Jesus said He could pray to the Father and be given more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:52-54) [1][2]. Where there is prayer there is angelic activity — prayer activates and releases angels [2].

The books also give examples: an angel came to Zachariah because his prayer was heard (Luke 1:8-16) [2][8], angels ministered to Jesus in the wilderness and in Gethsemane as He prayed (Luke 22:40-44) [3][6], an angel delivered Peter while the church gathered praying (Acts 12:1-12) [4], and an angel came to Cornelius, whose prayers rose as a memorial before God [4]. Daniel was told, "I am come for thy words" (Daniel 10) [6]. So expect angelic intervention because of your many prayers [2][8].

One other way the books name is hospitality — "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares," as with Lot and Abraham (Genesis 19:1-3) [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 6 of *Prayer Changes Things*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 19:1-3; Daniel 10:1-15; Matthew 26:52-54; Luke 1:8-16; Luke 22:40-44; Acts 12:1-12; Revelation 15:1.

items.question: How should I respond when people constantly accuse and criticize me for serving God?
items.book: One of You is a Devil
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this directly, and the first thing they say is to keep serving anyway. Most ordinary people do not feel qualified to serve God, and most of those trained in ministry were discouraged and accused by the devil, yet they were encouraged constantly to serve God and become priests in spite of their shortcomings [1][2]. Every attempt to serve God in ministry is a great and honourable effort, even though ministers are vilified and denigrated constantly [6].

When the accusation comes, you may need to answer it decisively rather than absorb it. David refused to accept Michal's re-description of his worship, saying it was before the LORD who chose him, and that was the end of the matter [8]. And do not let fear of accusation keep you from obeying the call, for fear is an evil spirit and following it leads to regret [3]. The books also counsel caution in receiving accusations: against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses, as 1 Timothy 5:19 says [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 5 and 8 of *Those Who Accuse You*, chapter 5 of *Weeping and Gnashing* and chapter 4 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 6:20; Isaiah 58:8-9; Daniel 10:13; Matthew 25:24; 1 Timothy 5:19; Revelation 12:10.

items.question: Can a pastor lead a group of people he pulled away from their church into a new one?
items.text:
Our books speak directly to this. The question every rebel leader must be asked is, "Can you lead these people?" and the answer given is no — the people you lead will never be loyal to you, because they have learned how to rebel and overthrow legitimate authority, and they will practise it again when they get the chance [1]. You will not be able to silence their rebellious way of speaking, quench their murmurings, or prevent the hatred and conspiracies around you, because you have sown the seeds of instability and rebellion and taught your followers how to dislodge legitimate leaders [1].

The books also show this working out in practice: a pastor who broke away and started his own church near the one he had led saw others follow his example, and a "domino spirit of rebellion" was released into the team of pastors [2]. One breakaway pastor appointed eleven new pastors of the lowest sort, as Jeroboam did, which makes nonsense of spiritual authority and confuses the flock [3]. And a pastor who left his associate over the old congregation later had that associate steal the hearts of the people and lead them away from him [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 5, 6 and 10 of *Those who leave you*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 12:28-31.

items.question: Why are Jesus' words so much greater than the words of other great teachers?
items.book: The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make
items.text:
The books say the words of Jesus are the words of the Son of God, and no other man ever spoke like He did — His words have outlasted any other words spoken by any other person [3][4]. Their greatness lies in their pure, lucid spirituality, dealing clearly and authoritatively with the great questions that throb in the human breast — who is God, does He love me, how can I be forgiven, where will I go when I die, how must I treat others — and no other man can answer those questions as Jesus answered them [1][7].

Where other teachers give truths mingled with what is trivial and absurd, He eliminated the trivial, the temporal and the false, selecting the eternal and universal [8]. His words are anointed, so that they changed the lives of those who heard them, for "the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life" (John 6:63) [5]. They are also full of love and kindness, teaching forgiveness not seven times but seventy times seven (Matthew 18:21-22) [5]. As those who heard Him said, "Never man spake like this man" (John 7:46) and "What a Word is this!" (Luke 4:36) [3][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *The Words of Jesus* and chapter 5 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 12:36; Matthew 18:21-22; Luke 4:36; John 6:63; John 7:46.

items.question: How do I know if God has hidden a gift in me that others can't see yet?
items.book: Lord I Know You Need Somebody
items.text:
What you're describing is exactly what these books speak about. Every great man of God is like a hidden treasure yet to be revealed, and God is the One who has concealed the potential He placed in you [1]. Your ministry is like a hidden seed planted in a field that will grow into a mighty tree, or like a little leaven hidden in a meal that will eventually influence the whole dough [1]. So the fact that people cannot see it yet is not a sign it isn't there.

The books also say that if you already perceive God has given you a gift, you are a candidate to receive even more, because "whosoever hath, to him shall be given, and he shall have more abundance" (Matthew 13:12) [7]. And the grace to see and hear is itself a gift from God, made by the Lord, as Proverbs 20:12 says [6]. So pray for the grace to see and hear, for if you are not into seeing and hearing, you are not into ministry [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Lord I Know You Need Somebody*, chapter 2 of *Seeing And Hearing* and chapter 12 of *Steps to the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 20:12; Matthew 13:11-12; Matthew 13:16; Matthew 13:31-32; Matthew 13:44.

items.question: Why does God allow trials and suffering in the lives of believers?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this directly, and they give several reasons God allows His people to suffer.

Suffering is appointed to us: it is given to us not only to believe on Christ but also to suffer for His sake (Philippians 1:29), and we are appointed to afflictions (1 Thessalonians 3:3) [5]. It pleases God to allow it, even as it pleased the Lord to bruise Him (Isaiah 53:10) [4]. It comes so we can follow the example of Jesus, who suffered for us and left us an example that we should follow His steps (1 Peter 2:21) [3]. It breaks the power of sin, for he that has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin (1 Peter 4:1) [3]. It proves we are good Christians, since those who live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution (2 Timothy 3:12) [2]. It goes along with our specific calling, as Paul said he suffered these things because he was appointed a preacher and apostle (2 Timothy 1:11) [1]. It tests us and humbles us, as Israel was led in the wilderness to be humbled and tested (Deuteronomy 8:2) [8]. And it is part of following Christ at all, for we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22) [7].

One caution the books add: a minister should suffer only according to the will of God (1 Peter 4:19), and it is important to seek His will about the suffering He allows, since there are two possible reasons for what you experience — you may be suffering according to His predetermined will, or you may be suffering the fruits of your own disobedience [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Losing, Suffering, Sacrificing and Dying* and chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing*.
