items.question: And how should I deal with them once I notice it?
items.text:
Our books give several methods. The first is the teaching method — teaching the Word of God regularly as a preventive process, because teaching fights against deception, and it is only people who are deceived who go the way of Absalom or Lucifer [6]. The second is the marking and avoiding method: Romans 16:17, 18 says to mark those which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine you have learned, and avoid them, for they serve not our Lord Jesus Christ but their own belly [2]. The third is dismissal — the biblical treatment for a mocker is expulsion, and failure to dismiss someone who must go is weak leadership, like allowing a snake to live under your children's bed [2]. This law rests on Proverbs 22:10, "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out" [7].

On dismissal, the books add that absolute evidence is not needed to deal with mysterious characters — being a mysterious person is deemed enough evidence for dismissal [5]. Disloyal, disobedient, non-compliant or offending bishops, pastors and workers should be dismissed completely even if they have been longstanding, since fellowship is a choice and no one must be forced to fellowship with those he despises or speaks maliciously about [5]. Yet in keeping with mercy and compassion, financial provisions should always be made for longstanding workers so they can live and work elsewhere without undue hardship, and they should be seen off properly so the root of bitterness does not spread in the church, as Hebrews 12:15 warns [5]. Questionable loyalty is diagnosed when a person makes malicious, damaging or poisonous comments, has a spouse or close relative who is openly disloyal, has close ties with an openly disloyal person, or communicates with persons who are openly disloyal [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 12 of *Those Who Are Ignorant* and chapter 77 of *The Gift Of Governments*.

items.question: How can I know what my calling from God is?
items.book: What It Means to Become a Shepherd
items.text:
What a good thing to be asking, pastor. Our books say you come to know your calling by watching and observing what the Lord does with you and through you — "ye see your calling, brethren" (1 Corinthians 1:26) — you watch what works, and you flow with what God is doing rather than waiting for a voice thundering from Heaven [1]. Your calling is also according to God's own purpose and grace, given in Christ Jesus before the world began (2 Timothy 1:9), so it is important not just to obey the call but to find out the purpose for which God called you [2]. And you must be filled with the knowledge of His will concerning your calling, since you can only be a teacher or sing or serve by the will of God, not merely because you like it (Colossians 1:9; 1 Corinthians 1:1) [3].

The books also say the call is highly specific — a door through which you enter ministry, not something certificates or connections can get you (Jonah 1:1-3) [4] — and that it is no accident but your predestination, so those who believe they are called take God's Word, their dreams, their visions and their quiet times more seriously (Romans 8:30) [5]. One of the principal manifestations of a divine call is a supernatural desire and interest in the work of the ministry (Hebrews 5:4; Romans 10:1) [7], and no one else has your calling; you must see yourself as someone with a specific mission that only you can accomplish [8].

items.question: How can I be a good shepherd to the people in my church?
items.text:
What a good thing to want, pastor. The books say plainly: if you are going to be a pastor, be a good one, doing it with all your might, as Ecclesiastes 9:10 says [2]. And they point to Jesus' own words in John 10 as the picture of what a good shepherd does.

A good shepherd leads his sheep by going before them — anything you want your people to do, you do first, so they see the ground is safe and follow, for they know his voice (John 10:4) [1][2]. He is known by his sheep and knows them, opening up his life so he is not a mystery to them, and keeping them so that none are lost, as Jesus said in John 17:12 [3]. He provides salvation for them by going out after the lost sheep, doing the work of an evangelist (Luke 15:4-7; 2 Timothy 4:5) [4][5][7]. He gives them life through teaching that brings wisdom and understanding, and he lays down his life and his time for them, as John 10:11 says [5][6]. He also notices when the sheep are in trouble and prays for their deliverance from witchcraft, demons and diseases, anointing them with oil [6].

The books also speak of being a door for your sheep — making a way for them to enter marriage, prosperity, and ministry through your teaching and guidance (John 10:7, 9) [8] — and of developing sheep in other folds and gathering your congregations together so they can hear your voice (John 10:16) [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 27 of *The Art of Shepherding*, chapter 13 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*, chapter 8 of *Church Growth* and chapter 2 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: Ecclesiastes 9:10; Luke 15:4-32; John 10:3-4; John 10:7; John 10:9-12; John 10:15-16; John 10:27; John 17:12; 2 Timothy 4:5.

items.question: How can I serve closely in ministry without missing the spiritual blessings?
items.text:
Draw near and stay near, for as James 4:8 says, "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you" [8]. Being close is both an art and an act of humility, and you are loved, wanted, and needed, so come closer and be as involved as you can [8].

When you are involved in personal service, make sure you get the "good part" — not the physical advantage, but the spiritual treasure, as Mary chose that good part which would not be taken from her (Luke 10:41-42) [1][2]. Be careful of being unspiritual around a spiritual person, and beware of familiarity, for even Jesus' own brethren did not believe in Him (John 7:5) [2]. Accept the spiritual opportunities that come with personal service, for the Lord ordained the twelve to "be with him" before sending them out (Mark 3:14) [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Rules of Church Work (2nd Edition)* and chapter 16 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: Mark 3:14; Luke 10:41-42; John 7:5; John 13:20; James 4:8.

items.question: How can I protect my church from wolves?
items.text:
The books give you several ways. Be a pastor on fire: fire, passion and zeal are killers of wolves, and Jesus baptizes with the Holy Ghost and fire (Luke 3:16), so a church that has lost its zeal is the one ravaged by ravenous wolves [1]. Be aggressive toward them, fighting the good fight of faith (1 Timothy 6:12) and showing wolves that you are too dangerous to attack [5]. Expect them and prepare: be sober and vigilant, because your adversary the devil walks about as a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8), and churches that do not teach loyalty and faithfulness will struggle to survive a wolf attack [4].

You can also place spiritual barriers. When you cannot physically protect the sheep, you may issue a spiritual perimeter curse as a barrier for the wolves, as Paul did against anyone preaching another gospel (Galatians 1:8-9) [2]. And identify those who sympathise with a "departee" and send them away, as Abraham sent away the sons of the concubines from Isaac (Genesis 25:5-6), since separation is often the only way to instil stability after someone has polluted the church [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 4 of *Those Who are Wolves* and chapter 10 of *Those who leave you*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 25:5-6; Psalms 31:18; Luke 3:16; 1 Timothy 6:12; 1 Peter 5:8.

items.question: Why do I need to hear from God for myself instead of just listening to my pastor?
items.text:
You need to hear from God for yourself because hearing Him directly is how you come to know Him — the more you hear from God, the more you know Him, and people are rejected because Jesus never knew them (Matthew 7:22-23) [1]. You may be in a good church with a good pastor leading the flock, but you will still need to hear the voice of God for yourself; if you do not hear from God directly you will get disconnected [1]. The children of Israel were brought to Mount Sinai to hear God's voice for themselves, and they failed that test [1]. You need to know God for yourself and not just through a second person [1].

At the same time, the books also teach that you should listen to the messages of your leader — to learn how to preach, as Hebrews 6:12 says to be followers of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises, and to use their messages as resource material to give you things to preach [2]. Hearing is about listening to the preaching of God's word, and the art of listening to preaching messages is one of the most important skills you can develop [3]. So the books hold both: hear God for yourself, and listen to your leader's messages.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Not A Novice*, chapter 4 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 1 of *Seeing And Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 20:19-21; Psalms 23:1; Matthew 7:22-23; Hebrews 6:12.

items.question: How do I deal with betrayal in the church?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this — betrayal in ministry is a real and heavy thing. The books speak to it plainly.

Betrayal is part of ministry and part of life; if you have not yet experienced it, you will, and it comes from people supposedly close to you [3]. Jesus' own familiar friend who ate His bread lifted up his heel against Him (Psalm 41:9) [3]. You are not greater than your master; Jesus was betrayed, and Paul was betrayed, so how can it be that you will not experience the same [4]? If Judas is anything to go by, one out of twelve people may be disloyal [4].

As for dealing with it: a disloyal associate operating freely is like allowing a devil to do what he wants in the church [1][2]. Jesus called Judas a devil, and a person who betrays you is a devil [1][2][6]. What God did to the devil — bound him, shut him up, and set a seal on him (Revelation 20:1-3) — is what you must do to the "Judases" in your life and ministry [6]. Do not deal with the enemy in a spirit of benevolence; be fierce and resolute, for all forms of disloyalty will end a church and a ministry [7]. Pastors who take disloyalty lightly live to regret it [1][2].

One method the books give is the teaching method — teaching the Word regularly as preventive management, since teaching fights deception, and it is only the deceived who go the way of Absalom or Lucifer [5]. Lay people who are loyal will also report what is going on in the congregation and help you overcome disloyalty [3]. And do not expect gratitude from man; expect your rewards from God [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *JUDAS
Who is he??*, chapter 2 of *One of You is a Devil*, chapter 5 of *Church Growth*, chapter 54 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 12 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*, chapter 33 of *Victory Secrets* and chapter 12 of *The Church Must Send or It Will End*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 18:7-9; 2 Chronicles 32:25; Psalms 41:9; John 6:70-71; Revelation 20:1-3.

items.question: What does the Bible say about enjoying the money and blessings God gives you?
items.book: Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich
items.text:
Yes, the books speak to this. Ecclesiastes 6:1-2 describes it as an evil when a man has riches, wealth and honour, yet God gives him no power to eat thereof, so a stranger eats it [4]. So spend money on yourself and use some of the wealth you have earned on yourself; that is part of enjoying your working life, and failure to eat your portion will make you hate life and hate work [4].

The blessing of the Lord is what makes rich, and He adds no sorrow with it (Proverbs 10:22) [1]. And God takes pleasure in the prosperity of His servant, enjoying giving you money because you are His servant [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 9 of *Rules of Church Work (2nd Edition)* and chapter 6 of *It Is A Great Thing To Serve The Lord*.

items.question: How important is it to actually obey what Jesus says?
items.text:
Friend, our books speak to this plainly: believing and obeying are not two things but one. "All through the Bible believing is equated with obeying," and to believe in the gospel is to pledge yourself to obey the commandments of God [4]. Jesus Himself said, "He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them, he it is that loveth me... and I will manifest myself to him" (John 14:21), so obedience is the sign of your love and it provokes the anointing; there will be no manifestation toward those who do not obey [2].

It matters for your whole life and ministry, not just your feelings. Adam's life and ministry ended because he hearkened to another voice instead of God's (Genesis 3:17) [3], and Scripture warns that those who obey not the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ face everlasting destruction (2 Thessalonians 1:7-9) [4]. Even a novice must learn the importance of obeying commandments, and since we constantly misjudge which instructions are weighty, it is important to just obey every single commandment [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Not A Novice*, chapter 8 of *The Anointed and His Anointing*, chapter 3 of *The Church Must Send or It Will End* and chapter 2 of *Faith Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 3:17; Deuteronomy 10:12-13; Matthew 22:36-40; John 14:21-25; 2 Thessalonians 1:7-9; 1 Peter 4:17.

items.question: How can I recognize when someone has gone from just being disloyal into open rebellion against God's servants?
items.text:
The books describe this as a process, not a sudden event. Disloyalty begins subtly with an independent spirit, where a person is still part of the church but does what he wants in spite of contrary instructions [4]. It then moves through stages until it reaches the open rebellion stage, which is the last stage of disloyalty [3][7].

At that open stage, a person openly attacks an authority figure he should rather honour [3]. He may openly attack someone he previously hailed and honoured, insult and accuse someone he has loved before, or dishonour dignitaries with inappropriate and bizarre words [1]. Such people spread preposterous lies and wicked stories to demean, debase and degrade God's servants, doing the exact opposite of good Christians who seek to honour God's servants [1]. The books also note that rebels desire alternative leadership, sometimes leaving a church in rebellion to seek appointments from other men of God [2], and that those who move from church to church always find something wrong with the leadership [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Those who are mad*, chapter 8 of *Those Who Rebel*, chapter 2 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty* and chapter 2 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 22:18; Deuteronomy 31:27-30; Joshua 22:19; 1 Samuel 15:23; 2 Samuel 15:11; 1 Kings 11:26; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalms 139:21; Revelation 12:9.

items.question: What is the difference between the true church and the false church?
items.text:
The true church, the bride of Christ, is always inviting people to God and saying, "Come to Jesus" [1]. The false church has no such message; instead it says, "Stay here, settle down, celebrate, prosper today, secure yourself, enrich yourself, make yourself happy" [1].

The books also warn that many large and popular ministries preach doctrines that sound like the Gospel but are not, and that large-scale deception comes to God's people through false prophets [2]. One mark that separates true ministry from false is the fear of God rather than people — a man-fearing shepherd's sermons and decisions are swayed by the people, while Jesus is the example of one who did not receive honour from men (John 5:41) [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *Make Yourselves Saviours of Men* and chapters 18 and 31 of *The Art of Shepherding*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:24; Jeremiah 29:31; John 5:41.

items.question: Why is it so important for Christians to be part of a church assembly?
items.text:
The books speak warmly to this. The assembly is where God meets needs — "the church is a place where needs are met," and all the needs of the people were met through the assembly [3]. It is also a place of protection: wild animals survive by staying together, and "once you are in church you are protected by the presence of the others" [2]. Scripture itself says not to forsake "the assembling of ourselves together" (Hebrews 10:25), and warns that separating ourselves is how people turn into mockers (Jude 1:18-19) [3][4].

It is also where you grow and are built up. The assembly is a place for edification — being built up in knowledge, understanding, morals and faith (1 Corinthians 14:2-4) [6], and revelation and knowledge are imparted there (1 Corinthians 14:6) [1]. Like a coal of fire, "you cannot survive on your own" (Proverbs 27:17) [4]. And assembling brings healing, for "the power of the Lord was present to heal them" when they were gathered (Luke 5:17) [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 6 of *One Thousand Micro Churches* and chapter 10 of *Key Facts for New Believers*.

items.question: Why should I be a soul winner?
items.text:
You should be a soul winner because it is the great commission, the great command given to us by our Lord Jesus Christ, as Matthew 28:18-20 says [2]. It is also the very reason Jesus came to earth: "For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost" (Luke 19:10) [7]. Soul winning is the heartbeat of Jesus, and it is how we imitate Him and become Christ-like [3][7].

Beyond that, people are wasting their lives away without Jesus, and soul winning gives them a chance to become new creatures in Christ, as 2 Corinthians 5:17 says [1]. It also brings great joy and energizes Christians, for the seventy returned again with joy (Luke 10:1-3,17) [5]. And one day we will rejoice over the seeds we have sown, for "he that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing" (Psalm 126:6) [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Tell Them*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 126:6; Proverbs 14:12; Matthew 20:16; Matthew 22:14; Matthew 26:27-28; Matthew 28:18-20; Luke 10:1-3; Luke 10:17; Luke 15:14; Luke 19:10 and 9 more.

It also brings great joy and energizes Christians, for the seventy returned again with joy (Luke 10:1-3,17).
And one day we will rejoice over the seeds we have sown, for "he that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing" (Psalm 126:6).

items.question: Why does God allow my enemies to stay instead of removing them?
items.book: WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous
items.text:
Our books give more than one answer to that, and I'll lay them out as they stand.

One reason is that God allows undefeated enemies to remain so His people can learn war and grow up in how to fight and survive; He left nations to test Israel, to find out if they would obey His commandments, as Judges 3:1-4 says [1]. The test of war is when God allows enemies to flourish around you so you have someone to spar with [1].

Another reason is that God uses your enemies for your good and promotion. He uses them as an audience to see your greatness and victories, as Psalm 23:5 says, and He uses their afflictions to work out good things in you, as Psalm 119:71 says, "It is good for me that I have been afflicted" [7]. Some of the greatest promotions come through enemies, and there are things you will not accomplish without having them [6].

A further reason is that God has determined to destroy them, and so He causes them to harden their hearts until the time of their judgment; the fight is not over because God wants them destroyed in the battle, as Joshua 11:20 says [5]. So do not be discouraged — God is going to right all the wrongs in your life [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous* and chapters 7 and 15 of *TS2. Hope Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Joshua 11:20; Judges 2:21-3:4; Psalms 23:5; Psalms 119:71; John 12:24.

items.question: How can someone turn to God in a moment of complete desperation?
items.text:
When things go from bad to worse, that is supposed to turn you towards God — your problems are meant to bring you towards Him, as the prodigal "came to himself" (Luke 15:17) [2]. Jonah, from the belly of the fish, cried out by reason of his affliction and said, "yet I will look again toward thy holy temple" (Jonah 2:1-4) [2]. So the call is to repent and turn to God — to arise and go to the Father, to return unto the Lord, for He has torn and He will heal, He has smitten and He will bind up [2].

And take heart: God is near to the depressed and broken-hearted — "The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit" (Psalm 34:18), and He is the God who comforts the depressed (2 Corinthians 7:6) [1]. He does not condemn people for speaking out their feelings in their time of depression; Jesus Himself was overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death and prayed alone to His Father [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 22 of *Those who are mad* and chapter 5 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 34:18; Psalms 118:9; Isaiah 31:1; Jonah 2:1-4; Luke 15:17-18; 2 Corinthians 7:6.

items.question: How can I tell if someone in my church is a false friend or a pretender?
items.text:
Our books speak to this, and they say plainly: you must judge by actions and not by presentation, believing the signs and symptoms the way a doctor reads symptoms of disease [2]. Watch for people who are too quiet, who seem to have two temperaments depending on who they are with, or who are too perfect and dignified in how they present themselves [2]. People who say nothing in your presence but talk a lot when they are away from you are good examples of pretenders — why have one picture when you are near and another when you are far [3][5]?

A Judas is a liar who pretends to be telling the truth, a destroyer who pretends to be building, a covenant breaker who pretends to respect agreements, and one who cannot be trusted but pretends to be the most trustworthy person around [3]. Watch also for someone you would expect to be angry and unforgiving because he was wronged, yet who seems to have ignored the offence and become even more gracious than before — be sure such a person has genuinely forgiven you [6]. And in times of pressure or crisis, notice who absents himself; it is in times of pressure that you see the true character of a person [8]. The Bible teaches us to prove all things and hold fast to that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5:20) [3][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1 and 2 of *Those Who Pretend, Intimidate And Are Familiar*, chapter 8 of *JUDAS
Who is he??* and chapter 5 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 27:21-24; Joshua 9:3-16; Matthew 23:27-28; John 7:5; 1 Thessalonians 5:20.

items.question: What does the fear of man do to a person spiritually?
items.book: Demons and How to Deal with Them
items.text:
Our books speak plainly about this. Fear is not merely a mood or an attitude — it is an evil spirit, and the presence of any kind of fear is a sign of demonic activity [3][5]. When Adam rebelled, fear entered the human race for the first time, and rebels are full of fear and insecurity [1]. Fear takes away the soundness of your mind, so that you behave abnormally and cannot love as you should [2][3]. As 1 John 4:18 says, perfect love casts out fear, because fear has torment, and the one who fears is not made perfect in love [7].

Fear also opens the door to many other evils — accusation, fault-finding, laziness, wickedness and poor performance — and fearful people become suspicious, accusative, insecure, and unable to take correction well [4]. It destroys love and manifests itself in suspicion and uncertainty [7]. The good news is that God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of love, power and a sound mind (2 Timothy 1:7), and David prayed to be delivered from all his fears (Psalm 34:4) [3][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Those Who Rebel*, chapter 4 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them*, chapter 26 of *Now We Are At War* and chapter 9 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 3:9-10; Judges 7:3-4; Job 3:25; Psalms 34:4; 2 Timothy 1:7; 1 John 4:18.

items.question: Can I still serve God while I'm busy with my studies or other responsibilities?
items.book: How you can become a strong Christian
items.text:
Yes, you can. The books speak plainly to this. Love for God is itself a guide: "You may be a student, but you will still serve God," and love for God told him to start a fellowship and preach even while a student [1]. He says, "I never put the work of God aside because of school," and that as a medical student he successfully combined his schoolwork with his pastoral work [3]. Being a student is just another "care" of this world which must not be allowed to choke God's Word and work [5].

The books also warn that the cares of the world — paying bills, family responsibilities, jobs, academic pressures — can choke the Word and make you unfaithful if they dominate your life [3][4]. So the call is to overcome these potential chokers and keep bearing fruit: "if you are too busy to be involved in winning souls, then you are simply too busy" [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry*, chapter 9 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 3 of *Bearing Fruit After Your Kind*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 22:13; Mark 4:19.

items.question: How do I become a better leader of people?
items.text:
The books say a good leader works on people until they become better human beings, and that being with a good leader changes your life forever [1]. That means leadership is not about titles; it is about changing the lives of those you lead [1].

Practically, they tell you to listen to people's problems and let conversations centre on others rather than yourself [6], to be an encourager and say thank you for everything [6], to smile, and not to be partial, since the wisdom from above is without partiality (James 3:17) [6]. They also say to value people, because people are attracted to places where they are valued and every person who feels undervalued will move away [7]. And they say to bring peace between people, following peace with all men (Hebrews 12:14), and to be at peace with those around you, since you cannot lead people with whom you constantly fight [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 20, 23, 121 and 126 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Ruth 4:15; 1 Samuel 1:8; 2 Samuel 18:3; Acts 4:13; Philippians 1:19; Philemon 19; Hebrews 12:14.

items.question: How can a pastor grow an empty church?
items.text:
Friend, our books speak to this. A pastor without anagkazo will have an empty church, and without it many churches will die a natural death; you must go out and compel people to come in, rather than sitting in church and inviting them [1]. The people who will fill empty churches are not in places where they receive polite invitation cards, so a new strategy of going to the gutters, highways and the bushes must be employed [1].

You must also fight for growth, for the gates of hell are postured against the church, and church growth is one of the most difficult things to do [2]. A burning vision for a large church is the invisible engine that drives a minister on that long and tortuous journey; in the absence of such a vision you will never have real church growth [6][8]. And remember the 80-20 principle: eighty percent of your increase comes from twenty percent of the people, so spend more time with the leaders and workers who will bring growth [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1 and 27 of *Church Growth*, chapter 11 of *Attempt Great Things for God* and chapter 13 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 29:18; Jeremiah 30:19; Acts 16:5.

items.question: How can I learn to work with different kinds of people to accomplish what God has called me to do?
items.book: What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent
items.text:
What a good question, and our books speak to it directly. The heart of it is that the number of different groups of people you can work with will reveal the magnitude of your calling — Nehemiah worked with forty-one different kinds of people, and Jesus came to die for all people, all kindred, all nations, all tribes and all tongues [1]. So assess yourself by how many different groups you can work with, and aspire to have the grace of Nehemiah to work with different groups of people [1].

Practically, the books name seven people you must learn to work with: your own church members, whom a pastor must both understand softly and challenge firmly; unbelievers whose expertise you need; people older than you, with carefulness and respect; lay people you do not pay, since volunteers feel happy when given a little task; women, if you are a man without sexual sin, or fellow women, if you are a woman, without quarrelling or jealousy; people who do not like each other but must work together, as Paul urged Euodias and Syntyche to be of the same mind in the Lord (Philippians 4:2); and technical people, by knowing a little about everything and asking many questions [2][4]. Peter had to learn this too, when God showed him he should not call any man common or unclean (Acts 10:28), and Paul became all things to all men that he might by all means save some (1 Corinthians 9:22,23) [5].

Two more things will help you. Your limitations in ministry are overcome by recognizing the contribution of others, for every joint supplies something until you become what God has called you to be (Ephesians 4:16) [7]. And becoming "another of the same kind" gives you access to methods and formulae that have worked for your kind — what worked for him will work for you — and it makes you a member of a group where you can fellowship freely with those who share your challenges [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *The Art of Following*, chapter 22 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*, chapter 14 of *Those who are Dangerous Sons*, chapter 100 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 6 of *Many Are Called*.

Scriptures referenced: Acts 10:28; 1 Corinthians 9:22-23; Ephesians 4:16; Philippians 4:2.

items.question: Can my friends keep me from staying close to God?
items.text:
Yes, friends can affect your closeness to God, though the books put the responsibility on you. They warn that "they that are far from thee shall perish," and that closeness is a test of your survival, so you must fight to be close to God and to those who matter [3]. The same passage tells you to learn from close people, watch what they do to come close, and not be one of the distant people who only say "hi" and "bye" [3].

But the books also say distance in the spirit is not about physical location: someone sitting six thousand miles away may be closer than you sitting at his feet, and God chooses those He allows to approach Him [1]. And nearness is measured by relationship, not proximity — you are close to anyone you talk to all the time, so a daily quiet time of talking with the Lord is what draws you near, as James 4:8 says, "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you" [3][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 16 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them*, chapter 6 of *WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous* and chapter 5 of *The Secret*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 65:4; Psalms 73:27-28; Mark 12:34; James 4:8.

items.question: How can they come back?
items.text:
The books speak of returning. God's own invitation is to reason together with Him, as Isaiah 1:18 says, "Come now, and let us reason together" [3]. Jeremiah repeatedly urged the people, "Turn away from your wicked ways. Stop doing evil! Repent and come back to God" [2]. And the warning is real: there is a certain line we must not cross, a point of no return, so the time to come back is now [3].

On the causes, the books name shallow roots, since some receive the Word with joy but have no root and fall away in testing, as Luke 8:13 says [2]; disappointment in a Christian leader, who is only human [1]; rebellion, which Scripture likens to witchcraft in 1 Samuel 15:23 [3]; sinfulness, for Proverbs 1:10 says, "if sinners entice thee, consent thou not" [4]; unresolved hurts and bitterness, which Hebrews 12:15 warns will trouble you [4]; not being committed to a church, for an uncommitted Christian is a potential backslider [5]; emptiness that invites the enemy to fill the vacuum, as Luke 11:25 describes [8]; love of the world, as with Demas in 2 Timothy 4:10 [8]; and a lack of prayer, since Jesus told His disciples to pray lest they fall into temptation [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 2, 7 and 8 of *Backsliding* and chapter 10 of *How you can become a strong Christian*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 118:14; Psalms 137:4; Isaiah 1:18; Jeremiah 2:21; Jeremiah 2:23; Matthew 22:8; Matthew 24:44; 1 Thessalonians 4:16-18.

items.question: Why do people who speak against God seem to prosper?
items.text:
Our books speak to this. Some people who are antagonistic toward God's work seem to flourish because it is determined that they should; they prosper "till the indignation be accomplished: for that that is determined shall be done" (Daniel 11:35-36), and even the threats against Jesus were gathered "to do whatever your hand and your purpose predestined to occur" [1]. The beast was given a mouth speaking great blasphemies and power to continue forty-two months, and then it was no longer allowed (Revelation 13:4-7) [6].

But the books also warn that apparent prosperity is not proof of God's pleasure. God allows people to stray into His imperfect will and then receive a fitting thrashing for their rebelliousness; He gave Israel their request but sent leanness into their soul (Psalm 106:13-15), and abundance and apparent success does not mean God is pleased with you [3][4]. Miriam was struck with leprosy almost immediately for criticizing God's servant (Numbers 12:1-15), yet many criticize today and seem to get away scot-free, even prospering [2]. Many sins are allowed to continue for years until the cup is full, and then judgment comes [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Predestination*, chapter 7 of *BEMA Judgment And Justice*, chapter 1 of *The Art of Hearing*, chapter 8 of *Those Who Are Offended* and chapter 26 of *Why Few Are Chosen*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 12:1-15; Numbers 22:9-22; Psalms 106:13-15; Daniel 11:35-36; Romans 13:1; Revelation 13:4-7.

items.question: How do I deal with disloyal people?
items.text:
The books speak plainly to this. Teaching the Word of God regularly is the first method, a preventive way of managing a church or business, because teaching fights against deception, and it is only deceived people who go the way of Absalom or Lucifer [3]. Beyond that, you must be fierce and resolute, not dealing with the enemy in a spirit of benevolence, for all forms of disloyalty will end a church and a ministry [4].

Practically, the books say to wipe out the associates of disloyal people, letting them go openly to the camp they love, since no friendship with a disloyal person is neutral [1]. The biblical remedy for a scorner is to cast him out, as Proverbs 22:10 says, "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out" [5]. Disloyal people are unfit for the work of God and worthless for good work of any kind [6], and you must handle them God's way, binding a "Judas" to restrict him rather than letting him operate freely [7]. Even longstanding workers who are disloyal should be dismissed, though financial provision should be made so they can live and work elsewhere, preventing the root of bitterness from spreading, as Hebrews 12:15 warns [8].

items.question: How can I escape the curse on this earth and start living in God's blessings instead?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this directly, and the answer they give is wisdom from above. God's wisdom from above is the master key to overcoming the curse on this earth, and anything in the Word of God is that wisdom — following any aspect of it will lift you above the curse [1][3]. As Matthew 6:33 says, seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added; when you set your heart on seeking God's kingdom, the supernatural power of God is released to make you prosper [3].

They also point to the anointing: the yoke shall be destroyed because of the anointing (Isaiah 10:27), and the master key to exiting a cursed path is to follow the direction of the Holy Spirit and to listen to the voice of God [4][6]. As Romans 8:14 says, as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God — you are lifted from a cursed existence into a supernatural one [3].

And they tell you to seek the blessing itself, for a blessing can counteract a curse no matter how strong it is [5][7]. As Deuteronomy 30:19 says, life and death, blessing and cursing are set before you; therefore choose life [7]. Seek these blessings, pray for them, and ask for a prayer and for hands to be laid on you [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 23, 24 and 31 of *How To Neutralize Curses*.

items.question: How can a young leader make up for not having much experience?
items.text:
The books speak directly to this. A young leader's main remedy is to study history: "The most important subject for a young leader is history," because a young person has to tap into the experiences of others, and his only chance of avoiding certain mistakes is to study those who went before him [1]. History is the greatest source of knowledge and wisdom, second only to the Scriptures, and the Scriptures themselves contain many history lessons that guide us [1]. As Ecclesiastes 1:9,10 says, there is no new thing under the sun [1].

The books also say experience itself is a teacher, and that allowing people to go through certain things is sometimes the only way to make their minds work in the right way — the Father even trained Jesus this way, for as Hebrews 5:8 says, He learned obedience through the things He suffered [7]. And an experienced person is simply someone who knows the difference between the ideal and the real, so do not despise the lessons of maturity you are learning [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 35, 40 and 124 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Ecclesiastes 1:9-10; Hebrews 5:8.

items.question: Can I get to heaven after I die if I know the right people?
items.book: How to be Born again & Avoid Hell
items.text:
No, friend. When you die you will discover that there is a big gap between heaven and hell, and people cannot cross over from hell to heaven no matter who they are or how much money they had on earth [1][2]. If you want to cross, you must cross now, because you cannot transfer when you die [1][2]. This will be hard for those used to getting things done through "whom you know," but salvation will be through the blood of Jesus and not through whom you know [1][2].

The rich man in Luke 16 found this out; between him and Abraham a great gulf was fixed, so that no one could pass from one side to the other [1][2]. And unless you are born again, you cannot see the kingdom of God (John 3:3) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 20 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*, chapter 4 of *How to be Born again & Avoid Hell* and chapter 16 of *People Who Went to Hell*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 5:13-14; Luke 16:25-26; John 3:3; John 14:6.

items.question: Why do people leave the church over small offenses?
items.text:
Our books speak to this. One reason is that unresolved hurts and wounds cause people to be cut off from their church; a man who came to a pastor admitted there had been "a slight problem" in his previous church, and the pastor recognized that his unresolved hurts had caused him to be cut off — this is one of the commonest reasons for people backsliding and leaving churches [8].

Another reason is shallowness: if you are not deep, you will fall away at the next shaking and crisis, and only a shallow Christian would fall away when a great man of God gets into scandalous sin [5]. Some also leave to avoid the confrontations of God's Word rather than admitting their sins and repenting — like the man who disliked his pastor's preaching on fornication because he was having an affair [3]. And some are simply contentious individuals who delight in magnifying frivolous and vexatious issues until these become a pivot for divisions [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*, chapter 3 of *Backsliding* and chapter 2 of *How you can become a strong Christian*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 1:10; Romans 16:17.

items.question: What does it mean that Jesus is a warrior king and we fight alongside him?
items.text:
Yes, friend, this is at the heart of our calling. Jesus Himself is the warrior King — He is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness He judges and makes war, with His eyes like a flame of fire and many crowns on His head [1]. He is even the Lamb who makes war, overcoming the kings who set themselves against Him, for He is Lord of lords and King of kings [2][4]. And when He rides out, the armies of heaven follow Him on white horses, clothed in fine linen, white and clean [1].

So if you want to follow Jesus, you join His army and you fight [2][6]. He Himself teaches our hands to war (Psalm 18:34), and we are told to fight the good fight of faith (1 Timothy 6:12) and to war a good warfare (1 Timothy 1:18) [4]. We are not at peace in the way the enemy would have us believe; anyone who thinks we are not at war lacks understanding [6]. And take heart — those who are with Him are called, chosen, and faithful [2][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in *Now We Are At War* and page 1 of *A Good General*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 18:34; 1 Timothy 1:18; 1 Timothy 6:12; Revelation 17:12-14; Revelation 19:11-16.

items.question: How can I make my faith stronger?
items.book: Name It Claim It Take It
items.text:
What a good question to ask, pastor. Our books say the principal way to improve your faith is by hearing: "faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God" (Romans 10:17) [2]. The more you listen to preaching and teaching, the more your faith is built up, so keep listening to messages you love over and over, old ones and new, and read the books God has placed in your hands [3][5][8].

Faith also grows when you use it — the scripture teaches that we gain by using what we have (Luke 19:15), so your faith grows as you use it [5]. And remember that faith is a variable condition; you must not let it be weak, little, dead or shipwrecked, but living, strong and rich [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Name It Claim It Take It* and chapters 14, 24 and 68 of *Faith Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 47:9; Luke 19:15; Luke 22:32; Romans 10:17; 2 Thessalonians 1:3; 1 Timothy 1:19; James 2:5; James 2:17; James 2:22; 1 John 5:4.

items.question: How do we know the Bible is really God's Word and not just written by men?
items.text:
What a good and honest question to ask, pastor. Our books speak to this directly.

The Bible itself tells us its origin: "no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost" (2 Peter 1:20, 21) [3]. It was "virtually written by God through the hands of mortal men," and "All scripture is given by inspiration of God" (2 Timothy 3:16) [2][4].

The books also point to evidence in the book itself. It was written by honest and godly men, because it condemns all sin and records the sins and faults of its own writers — something evil men would not do [1]. Its heavenly and eternal contents prove it to be of God [1], and it has been preserved through the ages, with whole kingdoms and religions seeking in vain to destroy it [1]. Even the wisest and most godly men acknowledge it as the Word of God [1], and one president put it plainly: "You will know the Bible is the Word of God when you read it: for in it you will find the key to your own heart, your own happiness, and your success" [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 7 and 8 of *Read your Bible Pray Everyday* and chapter 7 of *Key Facts for New Believers*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 119:9; Psalms 119:105; Acts 20:32; Romans 1:16; 1 Corinthians 2:14; 2 Timothy 3:16; Hebrews 1:1-2; Hebrews 2:1-4; 2 Peter 1:20-21.

items.question: What does the Bible say will happen to people who gossip and slander others in the church?
items.text:
Our books speak plainly about this, and it is a sobering word. A slanderer will not endure on the earth; evil will hunt him, and his stay will be cut short, as Psalm 140:11 says, "May a slanderer not endure on the earth" [1]. Slanderers are counted among the cursed, because disloyalty and blasphemy are equated, and the end of blasphemers is fire, brimstone, cursing and desolation [5].

There is also a word about the church. Psalm 15:1-3 describes who may dwell in God's tent: the one who "does not slander with his tongue" — so once a person has slandered the brethren, he can no longer be allowed to stay and dwell among us [1]. And the Lord warns, "Touch not mine anointed and do my prophets no harm" (Psalm 105:15), for it is a sin to campaign up and down spreading stories against God's servant [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 9 of *Those Who Are Slanderers* and chapter 9 of *Pillars of Loyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 19:16; Psalms 15:1-5; Psalms 105:15; Psalms 140:11; Revelation 13:4-7.

items.question: How can I receive a share of the Holy Spirit's anointing like the seventy elders did with Moses?
items.text:
What a good thing to long for. The books say plainly that you can become a partaker of the anointing of the Holy Spirit, and that the anointing can be shared — God took of the spirit that was upon Moses and put it upon the seventy elders [1][2]. But notice who did the taking and the giving: it was God who took the anointing and placed it on them, not Moses, and not the elders themselves [3]. So your prayers must be directed to God and not to the anointed man, for a man can receive nothing except it be given him from heaven (John 3:27) [3].

That said, God has chosen to place His mantle on human beings, and He does not seem to want to create a new anointing but to share and pass on what He has already placed on people [5]. So He will direct you to an anointed person, and you must respect and carefully handle him, because no one ever became anointed by God until he related properly with the anointed person [5]. The seventy elders were merged into Moses' ministry, bore his burden, and imitated him because they were united with him; by joining yourself to people who are anointed, you become anointed too [2]. Elisha clung to Elijah in just that way [2]. And be patient — everyone who received the anointing in the upper room had followed the Lord faithfully for several years, and the qualification for an apostle was to have been around at least three years (Acts 1:21-23) [8].

One caution from the books: you cannot engineer the anointing or shout it into existence, and wearing an anointed person's clothes, serving him, giving him offerings, or having hands laid on you will not guarantee that you catch it [3][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Tasters And Partakers*, chapter 10 of *The Anointed and His Anointing* and chapter 8 of *Steps to the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 11:16-17; Numbers 11:24-25; Numbers 16:1-4; John 3:27; Acts 1:8; Acts 1:21-23; Acts 2:4; Hebrews 6:1-6.

items.question: Why did the people on Malta first think Paul was a murderer and then change their minds to think he was a god?
items.text:
They first judged him by what they saw. When the viper fastened on his hand, the barbarians said among themselves, "No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he hath escaped the sea, yet vengeance suffereth not to live" [2][4]. They expected him to swell up or fall down dead suddenly [3][6].

But when they had looked a great while and saw no harm come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god [2][4][5]. Their thoughts about him shifted from dishonour to honour, and it was those good thoughts that opened the way for Paul to be honoured on the island [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 4 and 8 of *Those Who Honour You*, chapter 11 of *The Double Mega Missionary Church* and chapter 53 of *The Gift Of Governments*.

Scriptures referenced: Malachi 1:6-8; Acts 27:41-28:10.

items.question: Does sleeping too much really lead to poverty?
items.text:
Yes, our books speak to this plainly. Too much sleep and too much rest lead to poverty: "Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man" (Proverbs 6:9-11) [1]. Poverty comes like a traveller you cannot send away, and want like an armed man you cannot easily dismiss [1]. The same lesson is drawn from the field of the sluggard in Proverbs 24:30-34 — overgrown with thorns and nettles, its wall broken down [2][3][4][5].

King Solomon analysed poverty around him and concluded that much of it was caused by lack of hard work — that if sleep and folding of arms were dealt with, there would be more prosperity [4]. The books do add a caution, though: "I am not saying that all poor people are lazy," but some stay in poverty because they do not want to work hard [5]. And sleep itself is not the enemy — it is necessary for rest, relaxation, and productivity, and it is good to sleep as much as you can; it is *inappropriate* sleep, and sleeping too long, that the warnings address [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Awake, O Sleeper*, chapter 9 of *Why Is This Church Not Working?*, chapter 85 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 11 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 6:9-11; Proverbs 24:30-34; Romans 13:11-14.

items.question: A teenager in our youth group says he cuts himself when he is sad.
items.text:
This is a serious and painful thing, and our books speak directly to it. The madman of Gadara, under the influence of Satan, "cut himself with stones" — and this is described as a key manifestation of a self-destructive spirit [2][8]. Self-destruction is one of the strategies of demonic attacks, and the prodigal son is a picture of someone whose ruin was self-inflicted, as though he "cut himself with stones" [2].

The books also say that sadness that makes a person give up on life can only be demons [3], and that demons make people suicidal and tell them to destroy themselves [5]. Depression is described as a powerful spirit that can lead people toward suicide [4], and people with depression are suicidal [6].

So I would urge you to take this seriously and to pray for his deliverance in the name of Jesus, as the books call us to do [3].

items.question: How can wisdom help me when I'm facing a situation that seems impossible?
items.text:
Wisdom is the application of God's word to impossible situations, and it gives you grace to overcome where others would have drowned [1]. The poor wise man in the besieged city delivered it by wisdom, not by strength, and Scripture says "Wisdom is better than strength" (Ecclesiastes 9:14-16) [1][5]. So when you face something with no way out, wisdom is the key to solving impossible situations [5].

Wisdom comes through reading and through prayer — read Proverbs and Ecclesiastes and ask God for wisdom, for "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God... and it shall be given him" (James 1:5) [8]. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of wisdom, and through wisdom you can overcome impossible situations [3][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*, chapter 21 of *Attempt Great Things for God*, chapter 12 of *Daughter, You Can Make It* and chapter 84 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Ecclesiastes 9:14-16; Ecclesiastes 10:10; 1 Corinthians 1:24; James 1:5; Wisdom of Solomon 1:1-77.

items.question: How do I understand when Jesus says we must hate our father and mother to be His disciple?
items.text:
That is a hard saying, and our books treat it as exactly that — a difficult word that many cannot receive, and one that Jesus spoke as a real qualification for being His disciple: "If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple" (Luke 14:26) [2][4]. The books say there is a time and a place where you must hate your own father and mother in order to please God, and that perhaps you are not meant to understand it but to obey it if and when such a day dawns on your life [1]. They also warn that anyone who has eaten too much of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil will not be able to receive these instructions [1].

The books also say this teaching is reserved for those called at a higher level — teachings Jesus gave privately to His disciples and to ministers, not the congregational sermon of "love your wives" [3]. They note the apparent contradiction plainly: Scripture teaches us to love our wives, yet Jesus says you may have to hate your wife to be His disciple, and this applies to people who may have to hate their wives in order to fulfil their divine calling [1][3]. They also say the Bible teaches us to love our wives, but to love God first, and that many do not fulfil God's will because they try to please their wives [6]. And they press it further: if you must do that to qualify as a disciple, how much more as a Christian leader [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *The Tree and Your Ministry*, chapter 20 of *The Anointed and His Anointing* and chapters 1 and 2 of *Losing, Suffering, Sacrificing and Dying*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 2:9; Matthew 13:10-11; Matthew 19:21; Luke 9:58-59; Luke 9:61; Luke 14:1-35; 1 Corinthians 9:15.

items.question: Why doesn't God answer some of my prayers?
items.text:
I hear the ache in that question, and our books speak to it in a few ways.

Sometimes the answer is no because what we asked is not something God is presently doing. Jesus said, "The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do" (John 5:19), and He healed only one man at the pool though many needed help, because He dealt only with cases He knew would give positive results [1][2]. So God will have to say "no" when we ask Him for things which are impossible for Him to do [1][2].

Other times, sin is the barrier. "Your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden His face from you so that He does not hear" (Isaiah 59:1-2) [5]. He does not answer the prayers of disobedient children, but the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much (James 5:16) [7]. And answered prayer is linked to bearing fruit: "that whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you" (John 15:16) [7].

There is also mystery here. God seems to want us to keep asking the same things, and to pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17), yet He also calls vain repetitions what the heathen do (Matthew 6:7-8) [8]. The books say plainly that this is not easy to solve or answer [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 9 of *How to Pray*, chapter 5 of *100% Answered Prayer* and chapter 110 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 59:1-2; Matthew 6:7-8; John 5:1-8; John 5:19; John 15:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:17; James 5:16.

items.question: How can I receive an impartation of understanding from the Holy Spirit?
items.text:
What a good thing to long for, pastor. The books speak of this often, and they point to hearing with faith. The Spirit entered Ezekiel "when he spake" to him (Ezekiel 2:2), and the household of Cornelius received the anointing while Peter was still speaking (Acts 10:44) [2]. So expect an impartation when the anointed is speaking — in preaching, teaching, or even casual conversation — and be open to receive it [2]. Paul asked, "Received ye the Holy Spirit by the works of the law or by the hearing of faith?" (Galatians 3:2) [5][8].

Practically, the books say to keep listening, and to listen more than once: soak in a series of messages on an important topic until you are saturated, and keep listening to things you do not yet understand until you suddenly begin to understand them [8]. One writer listened to Kenneth Hagin for ten years before receiving the anointing to teach, and received the Spirit by the hearing of faith [8]. Also pray for the Holy Spirit — Jesus told us to ask for Him (Luke 11:13) — and pray for the spirit of wisdom and understanding, since the Holy Spirit is the spirit of understanding (Isaiah 11:1) [1][3]. A sudden great illumination of understanding is itself a sign that an impartation has occurred [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *The Anointed and His Anointing*, chapter 31 of *The Sweet Influences of the Anointing* and chapter 13 of *Seeing And Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 11:1; Ezekiel 2:2; Luke 11:13; Acts 10:44; Galatians 3:2; 1 Timothy 5:22.

items.question: What happens if I don't forgive someone?
items.text:
That is a serious question, and our books speak plainly to it. Unforgiveness is deadly if left unchecked: God will not hear your prayer, and He will not prosper or bless you while it lingers [1]. God will not forgive you for any of your sins, and none of your prayers will be answered, if you do not forgive [2]; as Matthew 18:32-35 says, the heavenly Father will do likewise to you if you do not forgive your brother from your heart [2]. The devil will torment you for your unforgiveness, and the tormentors can have access to torment you with sicknesses, diseases, poverty, and marital disharmony [2]. God will be angry with you, because He forgave you but you would not forgive others [1].

The books also describe where it leads over time. When hurt is not released it can degenerate into bitterness, and a bitter person's words affect, influence and poison others [7]. Malice—a desire to harm others—is a sign that you have not forgiven, and malice backfires; spite boomerangs, as Proverbs 26:27 says [4]. And unforgiveness blocks God's vengeance: He is desperate to repay your enemies, and the only thing blocking Him from unleashing that vengeance is your unforgiveness, bitterness and personal revenge [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 4, 5 and 8 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 130:4; Proverbs 26:27; Matthew 18:32-35; Romans 12:19-20; Ephesians 4:31-32.

items.question: What is blasphemy?
items.text:
Blasphemy is speaking reproachfully about God and His work — speaking impiously about God, His church, and His servants, and attacking their good reputation with malicious and injurious words [1]. It is also described as an act of cursing or reviling God, and the Scripture equates disloyalty with blasphemy, so that anyone who is disloyal is a blasphemer [2]. More simply, to blaspheme is to speak in an irreverent way about God or sacred things, and to show contempt or irreverence for God [8].

It is not only unbelievers who do this; born-again Christians can blaspheme with their tongues too, because blasphemy is also speaking irreverently about sacred things, and ministers of the gospel are in a certain sense sacred, having been set apart to minister the holy things of the Lord [6]. So when you accuse a minister of being a false prophet, a deceiver, anointed of the devil, or the like, you could be blaspheming [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Those Who Make Shipwreck*, chapter 9 of *Pillars of Loyalty* and chapter 6 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue*.

Scriptures referenced: Mark 3:22; Mark 3:28-30; Revelation 13:4-7.

items.question: How does the blood of Jesus cleanse me from my sins?
items.text:
Friend, the books say it plainly: nothing else can wash away the stain of sin — not soaps, not detergents, not even orange juice. Only the blood of Jesus has the power to wash away our lies, our stealing, our fornication and our murders [1][2][6]. As Acts 4:12 says, there is salvation in no other name [1][5].

The books describe it as a cleansing that goes one step further than forgiveness. You may be forgiven, yet there is often a scent of the past evils that contaminate us, so you need cleansing too — like the rescued man who was told, "Your life has been saved but you still smell bad!" [4][6][8]. As 1 John 1:7 says, the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin [3][4][7], and 1 John 1:9 adds that if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness [7]. The blood carries away our sin and filthiness the way blood carries away carbon dioxide [7], and through it we are washed from our sins and made fit for Heaven [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 12, 13, 14, 16 and 46 of *How You Can Preach Salvation* and chapters 3, 5 and 6 of *Blood Power*.

Scriptures referenced: Zechariah 3:3-4; John 6:54-55; Acts 4:12; 1 John 1:7; 1 John 1:9; Revelation 1:5; Revelation 22:11.

items.question: Does God want me to fight spiritual battles, and how do I do that?
items.text:
Yes, dear pastor, the books are clear that God does want you to fight. Jesus Christ leads the armies of heaven and makes war in righteousness (Revelation 19:11), and if you want to follow Jesus, you have to join His army and fight [3]. You are told to "fight the good fight of faith" (1 Timothy 6:12), and to prepare yourself to fight even more because you are a minister of the gospel [4].

As for how, you must accept that you will build for God and fight battles at the same time — that is part of the call, especially in this end time [1]. You fight with all your weapons: "Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil" (Ephesians 6:11), for the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds (2 Corinthians 10:4) [6]. And remember that your principal enemy is Satan and not other human beings [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *The Art of Following*, chapters 1, 3 and 60 of *A Good General* and chapter 4 of *Transform Your Pastoral Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: Nehemiah 4:17-18; 1 Corinthians 14:10; 2 Corinthians 10:4; Ephesians 6:10-11; 1 Timothy 6:12; Revelation 19:11; Revelation 20:1-3; Revelation 20:10.

items.question: Do pastors and church workers have the right to be paid and take time off?
items.book: Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)
items.text:
Yes, dear pastor, the books speak plainly to both.

On pay: a full-time church worker is employed by the church and should be considered for emoluments, benefits, accommodation, transportation, medical care, insurance and the like when the organisation is capable [4]. The Lord ordained that those who preach the gospel should live of the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), and the husbandman who labours must be first partaker of the fruits (2 Timothy 2:6) [8]. Paul asks whether a soldier pays his own expenses, or a farmer eats of his own crop, or a shepherd drinks the milk of his flock [2]. So do not be shy to earn money for the hard work you put in [8].

On rest: rest is part of God's plan for His cherished ministers, and vacations, days off and times of rest are their right [1]. Paul asked, "Or do only Barnabas and I not have a right to refrain from working?" (1 Corinthians 9:6) [1]. Full-time workers should have rest and leave periods, with the kinds of leave determined by the administrators and bishops [3][4]. In one church Mondays are the resting day, a little time of leisure and family respite [1], and Mondays can be taken as a day of rest and a day off [3].

One caution from the books: a lay pastor, volunteer or trainee is not employed by the church and must not be paid remuneration; any money given to them is a gift, not a salary [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)*, chapters 5 and 55 of *The Gift Of Governments* and chapter 38 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:22-23; Ecclesiastes 10:7; 1 Corinthians 9:4; 1 Corinthians 9:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14; 1 Timothy 4:15; 2 Timothy 2:6.

items.question: How do I heal from the hurts and offenses I've experienced in life and ministry?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak directly to this. First, expect that wounds will come — "if you are in the ministry, expect to be hurt and wounded by fellow pastors" [2], and "wounds and offences are part of this life" [5]. So the goal is not to avoid being hurt but to be healed, for "all spiritual wounds must be healed" [2], and you are healed "when you are no longer bitter" [2].

Practically, the books point to confession and prayer: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed" (James 5:16) [5][2]. And they warn against the path of withdrawal — separating yourself from other Christians "in the name of being cautious" leads to isolation from the body of Christ and backsliding [3][1]. The author himself chose to "allow the wounds in me to heal" rather than stay cut off [1].

items.question: How should an assistant minister behave during counselling sessions with the senior pastor?
items.text:
During counselling sessions, an assisting minister must not contribute any counsel that is contrary to what is being said, and must not try to develop a completely new train of thought, which may only confuse the one receiving counsel [1][2]. Do not try to impress anyone with some "high-sounding" wisdom; simply help your senior to say what he is saying better and emphasize what he has already said [1][2]. Do not remain quiet, because that will make you look like a spectator and make the counsellee feel awkward [1][2].

You can use simple but powerful phrases at intervals, such as "Do you understand what Pastor is saying?", "Do you understand that Pastor is only trying to help you?", "Pastor is only saying this because he loves you," and "I wish I had had someone speak to me this way when I was in a similar situation" [2][3]. As you interject comments like these, you lend a greater impact to his words [2][3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty* and chapter 3 of *Ministerial Ethics*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 18:16.

items.question: What should I do if I'm bitter about being moved away from a pastor who helped me?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this. Our books speak to this, and gently.

Bitterness is an advanced, deep-seated form of offense, and it can trouble you and defile many, as Hebrews 12:15 warns [2][3]. The way out is forgiveness: when you stand praying, forgive if you have anything against any, so that your Father in heaven may forgive you your trespasses, as Mark 11:25 says [8]. You can be liberated from bitterness as you forgive, and only then begin to experience joy again [8].

It also helps to talk about your pain with spiritually mature counsellors, pastors, or godly friends, confessing your faults one to another and praying for one another that you may be healed, as James 5:16 says — though after a while you must consciously stop talking about your pain, or you will wear your counsellors out and not make much progress [8]. And ask God to forgive you too, for He is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy, as Psalm 103:8 says [8].

One more thing the books note: people who struggle with being transferred from place to place are often agitated by spirits of rebellion, and it is pride that makes a pastor offended with a transfer [6]. I leave that with you to weigh honestly before God.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapter 10 of *Those who leave you*, chapter 16 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry* and chapter 59 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 14:31-32; 1 Chronicles 12:33; Psalms 103:8; Mark 11:24-25; Hebrews 12:15; James 5:16.

items.question: How does prayer make me stronger?
items.text:
Prayer is where your strength comes from, pastor. When you cry out to God, He answers and strengthens you with strength in your soul (Psalm 138:3) [2]. Every time you pray, your spirit is strengthened [3], and praying in tongues builds you up and makes you stronger, for "he that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself" (1 Corinthians 14:4) [1].

That strength is what carries you in ministry and in battle. Through prayer you receive strength to survive the attacks of the enemy, and the Lord stands with you and delivers you out of the mouth of the lion (2 Timothy 4:17) [2]. Prayer also gives you emotional strength, steadying your soul when your feelings would pull you the wrong way [2]. And when you pray, God gives you strength to overcome temptation and to do His will, so that you will not fall away [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 12 and 14 of *Pr 6. Prayer Opportunities* and chapter 5 of *How you can become a strong Christian*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 138:3; Proverbs 7:10; Matthew 26:41; Luke 22:41-43; 1 Corinthians 14:4; Ephesians 3:14-19; 1 Timothy 1:12; 2 Timothy 1:6-7; 2 Timothy 4:17.

items.question: How do I deal with demonic attacks on my family?
items.book: Demons and How to Deal with Them
items.text:
Our books speak to this. Attacks that involve stealing, killing and destroying are caused by the devil and his agents, and spending time to bind demonic powers and destroy their plans will protect you from such evil attacks [1]. When you deal with strife, quarrels and conflicts, you are dealing with Satan himself, so deal with the devil by dealing properly with anything that draws you into conflict [2].

It also helps to identify what you are dealing with, since demons and demonic activity must be identified in order to deal with them; ask God to reveal the real identity of the spirits [4]. Persistent attacks on your family, life and health are a sign of demonic activity, as in Job's case [5]. And you can tighten your security: staying with the truth and avoiding deception, practicing righteousness and avoiding sin, and emphasizing salvation all tighten the security of your spirit man against demons [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 8 and 18 of *One of You is a Devil*, chapter 20 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them* and chapters 5 and 24 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies*.

Scriptures referenced: Job 1:12; Mark 5:3; Mark 5:5; Luke 8:30; John 10:10; Ephesians 6:14; James 3:14-15; Revelation 16:13-14.

items.question: Can someone who gossips or slanders others still be a member of our church?
items.text:
Our books speak plainly to this. A slanderer will not be allowed to remain in the church, for Psalm 15 asks who may reside in God's tent and settle on His holy hill, and the answer is the one who "does not slander with his tongue" [1]. Once you have slandered the brethren, you can no longer be allowed to stay and dwell among us [1][2]. The instruction is to drive away slanderers, let them go, and not feel sorry for them, for you are better off without a slanderer [2]. A slanderer is a devil in our midst, and how can you accept a living, human, breathing devil into your fold [2][4]?

So do not receive people who come with stories and rumours against their former church, or who are filled with unverifiable, wicked stories about their last employer [2]. A slanderer separates close friends (Proverbs 16:28) and separates the sheep from their shepherd, causing members to fall away [4]. Such people are dangerous, and if discovered they should repent or be flushed out [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 9 of *Those Who Are Slanderers* and chapter 11 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 15:1-5; Psalms 31:12-13; Psalms 54:5; Psalms 140:11; Proverbs 16:28; Micah 7:8; Philippians 2:14; 1 Timothy 3:8.

items.question: Why is loyalty so important in ministry, especially during hard times?
items.text:
Loyalty matters because it is the principal qualification for every minister — "it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful" (1 Corinthians 4:2) [3][7]. It is not gifting, friendliness, or oratory that qualifies a person, but faithfulness and loyalty [3][7].

Hard times are where loyalty shows its true worth: in the good times everybody seems loyal, but loyalty is most appreciated in hard times [1][2]. Jesus told His disciples they would receive a special reward because they had continued with Him in His temptations (Luke 22:28-29), and their names are written on the foundations of the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:14) [1][2][4]. Those who stick with you through difficult times are different from those who come in when everything is working well [2][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 7 of *Why Loyalty?* and chapter 1 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Ecclesiastes 12:12; Matthew 25:21; Luke 22:28-29; 1 Corinthians 4:2; Revelation 21:14.

items.question: How does the Holy Spirit teach us today?
items.text:
The Holy Spirit teaches us today first and foremost as a teacher — that is His primary visible role, and Jesus promised Him to us as a Comforter who would teach us all things [3][4]. He makes Himself visible and relevant to us by teaching us all things, so when you read your Bible and begin to have deep revelations of the Word, the Holy Spirit is being manifest [3].

He teaches in several ways: He guides us into all truth, as John 16:12–13 says, and since God is where truth is, being guided toward truth is being guided toward Jesus [5]. He reminds us of everything Jesus has told us in His Word, bringing all things to our remembrance (John 14:26), and you do not truly know the Holy Spirit if you do not know Him as a "reminder" [8][1]. He also teaches through revelation — sudden bursts of revelation that are exciting and exhilarating, the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Him (Ephesians 1:17) [1]. He points us toward certain books we must read, as Revelation 10:8–11 shows [5]. And He speaks through people anointed to teach the word of God, so do not miss His voice that comes to you through an anointed teacher of the Word [5].

He also gives knowledge: through the knowledge of Him we receive all things that pertain unto life and godliness (2 Peter 1:3), and the knowledge the Holy Spirit gives us about God will lead us into everything that pertains to this life [8][4]. He may speak to your spirit, soul, or body — when He speaks to your spirit, you do not hear an audible voice; this is what people call "the inner witness" [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *The Love of the Spirit*, chapter 7 of *Amplify Your Ministry with Miracles And Manifestations Of The Holy Spirit* and chapter 10 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Nehemiah 9:20; John 8:32; John 14:26; John 16:12-14; Ephesians 1:17; 2 Peter 1:3; Revelation 10:8.

items.question: How can I tell when someone in my team is becoming disloyal?
items.text:
Friend, the books say disloyalty doesn't happen overnight — becoming disloyal is a process, and most people don't even notice it in themselves or in those they work with [1]. The first stage is an independent spirit: the person is still part of the church but does what he wants in spite of contrary instructions, obeying only the instructions he thinks are really important [1].

Watch too for the signs: people who absent themselves when the church is going through difficult times, since it's in times of pressure that you see a person's true character [2]. And watch for inflexibility — stubborn, defiant people who won't go beyond what is stipulated, won't adapt, and won't take correction when confronted, as Saul argued with Samuel even when the evidence of his disobedience was obvious [3]. The books also warn that people will pretend to you and tell you only what you want to hear, so a leader must not trust what people are saying wholeheartedly — Jesus did not commit himself to them, because he knew what was in man (John 2:24, 25) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 5 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty* and chapter 7 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*.

Scriptures referenced: John 2:24-25; John 7:3; John 7:5.

items.question: What should I read during it?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
Our books give a few ways to choose. You can choose a book of the Bible and read a few verses every day, always remembering where you ended so you can continue from the same place the next day — the author had wonderful quiet times reading through Luke and Ephesians in the New Testament, and Genesis and 1st and 2nd Samuel in the Old [5]. You can also choose a personality from the Bible and follow their life story, since a few verses about Moses will give you much revelation for your life [5]. Or decide to go through a particular book of the Bible every day, reading a few verses of a chapter and stopping exactly where the Holy Spirit seems to be speaking — stopping at every word, sentence or phrase that strikes you, and staying there to meditate until the full revelation comes [6].

You may also refer to your daily Bible reading guide, as these guides are very helpful in developing a regular quiet time habit and you will benefit from anointed teachers [4][8]. And as you read, recognize God as the author, for He has spoken to us by His Son (Hebrews 1:1, 2), and focus on Jesus as the central figure in the Bible [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *The Secret*, chapter 8 of *Key Facts for New Believers*, chapter 10 of *One Thousand Micro Churches* and chapters 11 and 12 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 34:1; Exodus 34:6-8; Psalms 119:18; Ephesians 1:17; Hebrews 1:1-2.
