items.question: What does it mean to be a shepherd over a small group of people?
items.book: What It Means to Become a Shepherd
items.text:
Being a shepherd means you see people as sheep and relate to them as such — a caring, loving guide whom God has called to look after sheep [1][3]. It is a specific kind of work: a shepherd is someone who has time to care, time to love, time to feed and time to gather the sheep [1]. That loving, caring and guiding is so real that the sheep end up calling their shepherds fathers [1][6].

Even over a small group, this is an honour: you are chosen from among men [2], you have a job in things pertaining to God [2], you relate to God directly on behalf of people [2], and you are chosen to have compassion on the ignorant [2]. Your assignment is to lead them by still waters and to green pastures (Psalm 23:2) [5][7], to guide them through wilderness situations (Psalm 78:52-54) [7], and to feed them, as Jesus told Peter, "Feed my sheep" (John 21:16) [4][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*, chapters 2 and 3 of *The Privilege* and chapter 20 of *The Art of Shepherding*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 23:1-2; Psalms 77:20; Psalms 78:52-54; Psalms 95:6-7; Matthew 9:36; John 21:15-17.

items.question: How should I respond to people who try to turn me against my church leaders?
items.text:
Our books speak plainly to this. Watch out for people who campaign against your fathers, trying to make you turn against your own father [2]. Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel from David, and the Scripture says, "So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel" (2 Samuel 15:6) [2]. Such people thrive on the ignorance and naivety of the people [2].

You must also be careful not to be drawn into confusion by strife-causing leaders, and you will be tested on your ability to silence the voice of the devil amongst your leaders and to mark and avoid dangerous people [3]. Do not be offended because a man of God you love and admire is under fire, for it is normal and expected for God's servants to go through fiery trials and temptations [6]. Those who love you will never believe bad things about you [6].

items.question: What does the Bible say about people who rebel against their leaders in church?
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this. A rebel is someone who defies authority, openly opposes leaders, disobeys their instructions, and gets into conflict and confrontation with authorities [2]. Rebellion is not a small matter: Scripture says "rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft" (1 Samuel 15:23), and it is a unique sin, distinct from every other [1][7]. The books also warn that God said He will not forgive rebellion, as Joshua 24:19 declares, "He will not forgive your rebellion and your sins" [7][8].

The counsel given is to reject rebels and have nothing to do with them, since Psalm 139:21 says to "abhor those who are in rebellion against you" [3], and Romans 16:17 says to "mark them which cause divisions and offences… and avoid them" [6]. Rebels are described as evil men who seek only rebellion (Proverbs 17:11) and as stubborn men with stiff necks (Deuteronomy 31:27) [7][8]. The books also note that rebellion can be against the Lord and His servants, and that when you defy God's servants you are defying God Himself [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapters 1 and 8 of *Those Who Rebel* and chapter 4 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 31:27; Joshua 1:17-18; Joshua 22:19; Joshua 24:19; 1 Samuel 15:23; Nehemiah 9:17; Job 34:37; Psalms 139:21; Proverbs 17:11; Ecclesiastes 1:9 and 1 more.

items.question: What difference does it make whether I serve the Lord or not?
items.book: It Is A Great Thing To Serve The Lord
items.text:
The books say there will always be a difference between those who serve the Lord and those who do not, and that you will return and see it [1]. One clear difference is in how your Father relates to you: the faithful servant was told, "All that I have is thine," while the prodigal was simply welcomed home [2], as Luke 15:31 says. The father also spoke of the son who would not serve as "lost" and "dead," while the one who served in the house was found and alive [2], as Luke 15:32 says.

There are other differences too: a difference in the covering over your life, so that you receive help from your father [3]; a difference in the outcomes of your life, for the prodigal became a beggar [3]; and a difference in the peace you enjoy [3]. Your status differs as well, for the older brother was a joint heir while the prodigal was no higher than a servant [4]. And if you do not serve the Lord, you will be handed over to serve your enemies, in hunger and thirst and want of all things [5], as Deuteronomy 28:47-48 says.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 4 and 10 of *It Is A Great Thing To Serve The Lord*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 28:47-48; Isaiah 65:12-14; Malachi 3:17-18; Luke 15:15; Luke 15:17; Luke 15:21; Luke 15:29; Luke 15:31-32.

items.question: How does God give revelation to people today if it's not always through visions?
items.text:
Yes, friend, the books speak to this. The spirit of revelation often manifests as visions and dreams, showing you what is happening behind the scenes [6]. But there is also what one book calls a "real life revelation" — John's ministry was birthed not only by visions but by what he had heard, seen, looked upon and touched, the Word of life (1 John 1:1, 3) [1]. So revelation can come through lived experience of Christ, not only through spectacular visions [1].

The books also point to meditation — thinking deeply about God's Word — as the ordinary path for most of us, since most will not have these special revelations and will have to depend on meditation [7]. And reading is another way: "Blessed is he that readeth" (Revelation 1:3), for a great blessing can come into your life by reading books [5]. One book even says those who have not seen and yet believe are blessed (John 20:29) [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Victory Secrets*, chapter 30 of *How To Neutralize Curses* and chapter 6 of *Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)*.

Scriptures referenced: John 20:29; Ephesians 1:15-18; 1 Timothy 4:16; 1 John 1:1; 1 John 1:3; Revelation 1:3.

items.question: How do I deal with people in the church who are disloyal or stealing from the offering?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to both of these plainly.

On disloyal people: you are to direct firmness at quieting, humbling, warning and controlling them [1]. Deal with all disloyal separatists the same way God dealt with Satan — throw them out, have no more meetings with them, and don't discuss their ideas and visions with them [2]. Even longstanding workers who are disloyal, disobedient or non-compliant are to be dismissed completely, though in mercy financial provision should be made so they can live and work elsewhere without hardship [3]. This rests on Proverbs 22:10, "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out" [5][6], and on the warning in Hebrews 12:15 about the root of bitterness defiling many [3]. Questionable loyalty — malicious talk, a spouse or close ties with someone openly disloyal — is itself grounds for removal, and that is not hatred but wise leadership [5].

On the offering: prevent the loss by monitoring who becomes an usher, keeping ushers in view, and ensuring security so no intruder can steal [7][8]. Have two or three count the money together, never leave anyone alone with it, use a signed form matching the bank pay-in slips, keep it in a secure safe, and bank 100% of it promptly — offerings should not be kept in the pastor's house [7][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *A Good General*, chapter 12 of *One of You is a Devil*, chapter 77 of *The Gift Of Governments*, chapter 8 of *Pillars of Loyalty*, chapter 10 of *Church Growth* and chapter 3 of *Church Administration*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 15:11; Proverbs 22:10; Titus 1:5; Hebrews 12:15.

items.question: What happens to a person who dies without being born again?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak plainly to this. When you die you will either go to Heaven or Hell — you will not just stop existing, but head for a permanent destination away from this earth [4]. The rich man in Luke 16:22-23 died and in hell he lifted up his eyes, being in torments, while Lazarus was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom [4].

The reason is that sin came into the world through one man, and death as the result of sin spread to all men because all sinned (Romans 5:12), so every unsaved soul is bound to end up in hell [2]. Unless a man is born again spiritually and reconciled to God through Christ, he is headed for Hell [2]. And it is the soul that goes to Hell; your spirit and your soul will suffer there [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *People Who Went to Hell* and chapters 3 and 4 of *How to be Born again & Avoid Hell*.

Scriptures referenced: Jeremiah 17:9; Mark 8:36; Luke 16:19-31; Romans 1:18; Romans 5:12.
